# How Facebook uses the email or mobile phone number on your profile

Copy link

How does Facebook use my email?

How does Facebook use my phone number?

How do I add Facebook contact info?

What is Facebook's privacy policy?

I have a different question

 We’re gradually updating people to [Meta Accounts](https://l.facebook.com/l.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.meta.com%2Fhelp%2Fmeta-account%2F876751767182450%3Fhelpref%3Dfaq_content&h=AUCvsb6UTXy3vWtdgoqWKQO-aHM1YgdQY5ngQ4CMGFJrZG96vQMCkJbAxBjglheEugjAE6T_kM-vfSNG21q5P7FaH140jcHP2lU3q5fEBvK035vLgI02D3INcdUcWC_5NjAALkbc2MdEbg). You may see either Accounts Center or Meta Account settings as the place to manage your account settings.

## How we use your email address or mobile phone number

We may use your email address or mobile phone number for purposes like:

*   [Helping you log in](https://www.facebook.com/help/283100488694834?helpref=faq_content). If you forget your password, you'll need an updated phone number or email address to reset it. If you forget or [lose access](https://www.facebook.com/help/132243923516844?helpref=faq_content) to the email address or phone number associated with your account, you can use one to look up the other. 
*   Sending you email, WhatsApp and SMS notifications for updates about activity on your account, promotions and account safety. These notifications can help keep your account safe through features like two-factor authentication and alerts about unrecognized logins.
*   Providing and improving ads for you and others. We use your contact information alongside information we get from your activity to help us improve our ads services for everyone within the Facebook community.
*   Some of our security checkpoints can be difficult to pass using assistive technology. If you add a mobile number or email address to your Facebook account, you'll have another way to verify your account if you need to pass any of these checkpoints. Keep in mind that these checkpoints may require internet access. 

By entering your phone number, you authorize your mobile network provider to share data from your account and device to Facebook or its service providers for phone number verification and fraud prevention purposes. Learn more about the data we collect and how we use it in our [Privacy Policy](https://www.facebook.com/privacy/policy/).

We never sell personal information, including your email address and phone number, to anyone. Keep in mind that you can control who can [see your contact information](https://www.facebook.com/help/117118145038822?helpref=faq_content) and who we can [suggest your profile to](https://www.facebook.com/help/131297846947406?helpref=faq_content) based on your phone number or email address. Learn more about how Facebook uses your phone number and email address in our [Privacy Policy.](https://www.facebook.com/about/privacy)

You may see an email or phone number suggested for you when we ask you to add your contact information. Emails or phone numbers shown in this way will only be added to your account if you choose to [add them](https://www.facebook.com/help/223900927622502?helpref=faq_content).

## How we suggest email addresses or phone numbers

We may suggest an email address or phone number for you based on information we receive from sources such as: 

*   Contact information provided by others on Facebook.
*   An email address or phone number that you entered previously but didn't confirm.
*   Your mobile phone or tablet.

## Reasons for confirming your mobile phone number

We may ask you to confirm your mobile phone number because:

*   You previously [added the phone number](https://www.facebook.com/help/297947214257999?helpref=faq_content) we're asking you to confirm.
*   Time has passed since you last added or updated your phone number.
*   We’ve received information from your device that helps us suggest the number connected to that device.
*   You haven’t added one yet, and we want to show you how.

## More information

*   [Add or remove a mobile phone number.](https://www.facebook.com/help/124895950923762?helpref=faq_content)
*   [Add or remove an email address.](https://www.facebook.com/help/162801153783275?helpref=faq_content)
*   [Adjust how you get notifications.](https://www.facebook.com/help/390022341057202?helpref=faq_content)
*   [Recover your Facebook account if you can't access your account email address or mobile phone number.](https://www.facebook.com/help/132243923516844?helpref=faq_content)

Meta Pay

Meta Pay is an easy, secure way to pay on the apps you already use.

Not in the US? [Check availability](https://l.facebook.com/meta-pay/availability/)

![Image 3: Easy Checkout](https://lookaside.fbsbx.com/elementpath/media/?media_id=3486918374891602&version=1741847833)

Shop, donate or send money on the apps you already use

When you use Meta Pay, it loads your saved payment, shipping, and contact information automatically so you can check out quickly.

![Image 5: Check out easily](https://lookaside.fbsbx.com/elementpath/media/?media_id=2095010837510412&version=1741858205)

## Check out easily and quickly

Use Meta Pay when shopping online. If you have Meta Pay set up, your saved payment, shipping, and contact information loads automatically after a quick Facebook or Instagram login verification.

New to Meta Pay? [Add your payment method](https://www.facebook.com/help/503055570507753) once and you'll enjoy a fast checkout every time you use Meta Pay.

![Image 6: Payment management](https://lookaside.fbsbx.com/elementpath/media/?media_id=363669089633515&version=1743144654)

## Manage your payment activity

You can easily manage payment methods, view your payment and transaction history, or access customer support in [Accounts Center](https://www.facebook.com/help/943858526073065).

Your security and protection matter

![Image 7: Anti fraud monitoring](https://lookaside.fbsbx.com/elementpath/media/?media_id=244195221960097&version=1743144654)

![Image 8: Customer support](https://lookaside.fbsbx.com/elementpath/media/?media_id=748828830473261&version=1743144654)

![Image 9: Data security](https://lookaside.fbsbx.com/elementpath/media/?media_id=216003424836249&version=1743144654)

### Anti-fraud monitoring

To detect unauthorized activity, payments are monitored using anti-fraud technology.

[Learn more](https://www.facebook.com/help/2167164950254129)

### Customer support

If an unauthorized Meta Pay transaction appears on your bank account, customer support is always ready to help. Chat live 24 hours a day or reach out via email.

[Learn more](https://www.facebook.com/help/218846068134280)

### Data security

To keep your information secure, your debit and credit card numbers are encrypted for safe and secure storage.

[Learn more](https://www.facebook.com/help/663265547498941)

### Open your favorite app

Start a payment on the apps, such as Facebook, Messenger and Instagram, you already use. There's no need to download a separate app.

### Enter your payment details

Add the credit card, debit card or PayPal account you’d like to use. You can update your preferred payment method any time within Meta Pay settings.

### Create a PIN for Meta Pay

Protect yourself from unauthorized transactions with a personalized PIN to control access. Once it’s enabled, you will be prompted to enter it before some purchases for additional security.

### Manage your payment information

Manage and update your preferred payment method in Accounts Center at any time. You can also view your transaction history across all connected apps in the same Accounts Center.

### Send money

When you're sending money to friends and family, the money goes straight into the recipient’s bank account. There’s no waiting and no fees.

(There may be fees imposed by your bank which are separate from Meta Pay.)

## Use Meta Pay seamlessly between Facebook and Instagram

Set up Meta Pay on Facebook by adding your preferred payment just once, then connect it across Instagram without having to re-enter your information each time.

## FAQs

We’ve included some frequently asked questions below. For more, visit [Meta Pay Help Center](https://pay.facebook.com/faqs/#General).

How does Meta Pay work?

Meta Pay is a seamless and secure way to make payments on Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, and in participating online stores. Enter your payment card or account information just once and then use Meta Pay to make purchases, send money or donate. Add a PIN or use the fingerprint or face ID on your device to secure individual payments. Meta Pay also lets you view your payment history, manage payment information and access 24-hour chat service for customer support.

Is it secure to make payments with Meta Pay?

We use advanced technology to keep payment information secure. Meta Pay is protected with:

*   Anti-fraud technology that monitors purchases on Meta Pay systems to detect unauthorized activity.
*   Payment card numbers are securely stored, encrypted and stored separately from your profile data.
*   Notifications that alert you if Meta Pay detects unusual activity.
*   An option to create a PIN or use the fingerprint or face ID on your device for additional security when sending money or making a payment. Facebook does not receive or store your device’s biometric information.

How do I set up a Meta Pay PIN?

When making a payment with Meta Pay, you may be required to set up a PIN (PIN is mandatory in some use cases) by selecting a 4-digit numeric pass code. You may also be able to use your device's face ID or fingerprint for an extra layer of security.

You can also set up a PIN with Meta Pay for additional security when sending payments by going to Orders and Payments settings. As part of our commitment to security, we may prompt a PIN with Meta Pay verification when certain types of transactions appear as unusual activity.

Do I need to have a Facebook account to use Meta Pay?

Meta Pay can be set up by logging into at least one of our apps - Facebook, Instagram or Messenger. Then, enter your payment card or account information. When Meta Pay is set up on Facebook and Messenger, people can connect Meta Pay across Instagram without having to re-enter their payment information.

Where can I use Meta Pay?

Meta Pay can be used on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, and in participating online stores.

*   On **Facebook**, you can use Meta Pay to shop, donate, buy tickets for events, or games.
*   On **Instagram**, you can use Meta Pay to shop or make donations to charitable or personal fundraisers.
*   On **Messenger**, you can use Meta Pay to send money to friends and family in the United States.
*   When online stores have Meta Pay enabled, you can shop the products and services you love, and check out faster with your saved credentials.

Meta Pay may not be available in all payment use cases on Facebook, Instagram and Messenger. We are continuing to build out functionality so that more people in more places can use Meta Pay across our technologies. Check back here for updates.

## About this app

_arrow\_forward_

Keeping up with friends is faster and easier than ever with the Facebook Lite app! Use Facebook Lite as a friends app to connect and keep up with your social network. The Facebook Lite app is small, allowing you to save space on your phone and use Facebook in 2G conditions. Many of the classic features of Facebook are available on the app, such as sharing to a Timeline, liking photos, searching for people, and editing your profile and groups. Specific features include:  
  
 • Find friends and family  
 • Post status updates & use Facebook emoji to help relay what’s going on in your world  
 • Share photos and your favorite memes  
 • Get notified when friends like and comment on your posts  
 • Find local social events, RSVP, and make plans to meet up with friends  
 • Interact with your friends by adding your own comments or reactions to their Facebook posts  
 • Save photos by adding them to photo albums  
 • Follow people to get their latest news  
 • Look up local businesses to see reviews, operation hours, and pictures  
 • Buy and sell locally on Facebook Marketplace  
  
The Facebook app does more than help you stay connected with your friends and interests. It's also your personal organizer for storing, saving and sharing photos. It's easy to share photos straight from your Android camera, and you have full control over your photos and privacy settings. You can choose when to keep individual photos private or even set up a secret photo album to control who sees it.  
  
Facebook Lite also helps you keep up with the latest news and current events around the world. Subscribe to your favorite celebrities, brands, websites, artists, or sports teams to follow their News Feeds from the convenience of your Facebook Lite app!

Bengaluru has overtaken Mumbai as the city with the highest traffic congestion and emerged on top of the list globally. According to TomTom Traffic Index, a major global location technology specialist, drivers in the southern city spent an average of 71% extra time on the road due to congestion in 2019, while in Mumbai, drivers spent 65% more time in traffic.

![Image 2: Bengaluru has world’s worst traffic congestion, Mumbai at number 4](https://static.toiimg.com/thumb/msid-73747764,imgsize-511672,width-400,resizemode-4/73747764.jpg)

Motorists stranded in a traffic jam on Swami Vivekananda Road, Halasuru, heading towards MG Road in Bengaluru (File photo)

NEW DELHI: Bengaluru has overtaken Mumbai as the city with the highest traffic congestion and emerged on top of the list globally.  
According to a report released by a major global location technology specialist, drivers in the southern city spent an average of 71% extra time on the road due to congestion in 2019, while in Mumbai, drivers spent 65% more time in vehicles thanks to the city’s traffic snarls.

The ninth edition of TomTom Traffic Index saw Pune, which was included for the first time in 2019, ranked fifth where drivers spent 59% extra time because of traffic jams. Indian cities were included in the global ranking for the first time in 2017.  

![Image 5: Delhi clogged roads](https://static.toiimg.com/thumb/imgsize-23456,msid-73754301,width-600,resizemode-4/73754301.jpg)

  
Friday evening (7-8 pm) was the worst period for commuters in Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru. One could save up to five hours annually for a 30-minute commute by deferring the journey post-8pm on these days.  
According to the report, on average, Delhiites driving during peak hours spent an extra 190 hours or seven days and 22 hours in traffic during 2019. In the case of drivers in Bengaluru, the extra time spent on roads was 243 hours or 10 days and 3 hours while time wasted in congestion on Mumbai roads was equivalent to 8 days and 17 hours.   
In Delhi, roads were most congested on Oct 23 last yr  
Pune commuters wasted around 8 days and one hour due to idling on roads. The report says October 23 last year saw the worst traffic congestion on Delhi’s streets. One of the major reasons for acute congestion in Delhi was the protest by nearly 200 physically challenged people, who had taken over Mandi House, leaving central Delhi gridlocked. The protesters were demonstrating against the railways for failing to give them jobs.  
Mumbai witnessed its worst traffic jam on September 9 while in Pune, August 2 was the worst day for the commuters on the city roads.   
In the case of Bengaluru, August 20 saw maximum traffic congestion. “We get the data from multiple sources across the globe and in every few seconds, we get updates from nearly 600 million devices,” said TomTom’s strategic business development manager, [Vinod Kumar](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/topic/vinod-kumar).

# Cinemas Paradiso

A number of the world’s most glamorous Art Deco theaters remain emblems of our cinematic dreams

![Image 2](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/7Cy6S1GeB8W16reFdft0z8/b32e167a6938edbc6f2f890f5799a738/Hero_Opener_3.5.21_2.png?w=2400&fm=webp&q=75)

Category:[Culture](link_6)

Location:[Egypt](link_7)

Words by:

[PRIOR Team](link_8)

Photography:Angela Witmore

Published March 5, 2021

Few existing architectural symbols capture the boom of Hollywood’s nascent cinema industry more evocatively than Art Deco theaters. These emerged in the 1920s and ‘30s as Art Deco and Art Nouveau were reaching their zeniths, but also in the midst of other historic milestones: the Flapper Era, the Suffragist Movement, Paris’ ascent on the global artistic stage and, of course, the Great Depression. With their facades boldly festooned in heraldic chevrons and courtly colonnades, Art Deco theaters across the globe stood as symbols of the interwar era’s cultural and commercial optimism.

Often seating thousands, these temples of high and pop culture emerged as essential gathering spots for the urban affluent and entertainment-hungry masses. They also often contained technological wonders like air-conditioning, elevators and parking, still rarities at the time. These cultural centers offered the public an escape from the urban chaos to lose themselves in the grandeur and romance that only Hollywood can deliver—all accented by the Deco era’s futuristic splendor.

![Image 3: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/5m7ZdbvJipfgA3KdDxbcbz/b526e16c6f7a763112847e11a5d27928/Content_Portrait_Intro_Cinema_Rif_in_Tangiers__image_by_Conor_Burke.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

Inside Cinéma Rif in Tangier, Morocco. Photo by Conor Burke.

Many of the most elaborate of these Art Deco gems have been destroyed or repurposed—the Odeon Marble Arch in London was demolished in 1964 to make way for a widescreen cinema, while the curvilinear Alhambra in Tel Aviv is now consecrated to another Hollywood fixation as a Church of Scientology center. But many still stand strong—some even continuing to show films, others now used as performance halls. Whatever their contemporary function, these enduring beauties are still worth a visit to take in their mix of Art Deco flavor meshed with local culture and materials. Here are a few worth flying for.

## Los Angeles: Grauman’s Egyptian Theatre

No cinema better evokes Hollywood’s Deco-era lore like the Grauman’s Egyptian Theatre in Los Angeles. Built in downtown L.A. in 1928, it was designed in a Deco-meets-Pharaonic style now known as Neo-Egyptian, with hieroglyphs inside and out, along with four massive columns fronting the theater’s main entrance—each more than 20 feet wide. Home to the first-ever movie premiere (_Robin Hood_ in 1922), it’s now owned, of course, by Netflix, which intends to use the space for special film events.

![Image 4: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/3PxCoXNhGhW1odS3AGObuY/c92e523b9cd2883734b1f4bebeadd3fa/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_Intro_2_Wikipedia_Egyptian_Theater__Los_Angeles.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

The Grauman’s Egyptian Theatre in Los Angeles.

## Mexico City: Cine Metropólitan

In the historic Centro district, the 1943 Cine Metropólitan—which originally held 3,600 seats—is fittingly grand for a city of 20 million. It debuted as a movie theater with a linear Art Deco facade by Mexican architect Pedro Gorozpe; interiors are French neoclassical, with gilded corinthian columns and oil paintings depicting aristocratic life. In the ‘50s, it became _the_ place for children in Mexico City to watch Disney movies; today it’s a concert venue known as the Teatro Metropolitan.

![Image 5: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/1Z4kECVpQO0MryUNa16xGp/3e9923803c0c40b93b6edb0a263656a4/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_2_Wikipedia_Metropolitan__Mexico_City.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

Cine Metropólitan in Mexico City.

## Oakland, CA: The Paramount

The 1931 Paramount Theater stands as a symbol of its own glory, having once prevailed as the Bay Area’s most influential cinema. Built by Timothy Pflueger, the San Francisco architect behind the city’s Pacific Coast Stock Exchange, the Paramount was acquired by the City of Oakland, which oversaw a meticulous restoration that preserved most of its Deco details—zig-zagged flooring and swirling ceiling lights. Today it hosts a robust film schedule and is home to the Oakland Symphony Orchestra.

![Image 6: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/5j7drdxzzmXlyP5HoPiq6I/3ec61757bd99751f1dd4ae46e5e3b590/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_3_Wikipedia_Paramount__Oakland__CA.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

The Paramount in Oakland, California.

## Istanbul: Süreyya Opera House

Set in Istanbul’s upscale Kadıköy district near the Bosphorus, the 1920s-era Süreyya is distinguished by its carved-stone facade evoking European Belle-Epoque designs. The interiors are Art Deco dreamscapes, with richly-inlaid ceiling murals, curved balustrades and Tiffany-style chandeliers. Though the Süreyya was envisioned as a place for opera and musical theater, it had a colorful history as a site for weddings, plays and a cinema; today, the Istanbul State Opera and Ballet commands the stage.

![Image 7: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/4Oc3gBUFFbepg7wJNeggfS/4032714bd4a31efb8ca24fc1578e144c/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_4_Flickr_Su__reyya_Opera_House.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

Süreyya Opera House in Istanbul, Turkey.

## Mumbai: The Regal

In the 1930s, when Mumbai rose as India’s answer to Hollywood, the Regal was the city’s most glorious Art Deco cinema. It debuted in 1933 on the busy Colaba Causeway, and, according to lore, was India’s first fully air-conditioned theater. The Regal’s concrete exterior is topped by a ziggurat-style crown; interiors are lined in elaborate Czech mirrors, orange and jade-green sunray motifs and _bas_-relief theatrical masks flanking the massive movie screen, which still regularly shows films.

![Image 8: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/5rKii54zuEywdpD57XtQBb/32c17b3645c331f2dbfeaa5974fbf67d/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_5_Flickr_Regal_Mumbai__image_by_Gioconda_Beekman.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

The Regal in Mumbai. Photo by Gioconda Beekman.

## Casablanca: Cinema Rialto

During the early 20th-century French Protectorate era, shining examples of Art Deco proliferated across Morocco, among them the lattice-fronted Cinema Rif in Tangier. In Casablanca, the 1929 Cinema Rialto is also an Art Deco icon, its name prominently etched on a swish red-and-ochre facade and its roof capped by a cupola. With a single screen facing 1,350 plush red seats, the Rialto was always (and still is) a movie theater, but has also welcomed the likes of performers Edith Piaf and Josephine Baker.

![Image 9: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/3eewrk2mkXNS4xVSK9i1kR/4c520a74caa7384399fed216b811d298/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_6_Flickr_Rialto__Casablanca__image_by_Jean-Franc__ois_Gornet.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

Cinema Rialto in Casablanca, Morocco. Photo by Jean-François Gornet.

## Sydney: Golden Age Cinema

The Golden Age Cocktail Bar and Cinema may now be a place where you can catch a classic film while enjoying a craft cocktail, but it began life as the Deco-divine home of Paramount Pictures in Australia. Completed in 1940, the building—set in the affluent Surrey Hills district—was both a film house and office block, all devoted to movies. Paramount House has been thoroughly updated, though it retains its elegant brass windows, cut-glass chandeliers and its streamlined, nautical-inspired facade.

![Image 10: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/4h1TkULZc29moY6k0fbZlH/69941404734cc450533a6da3d929c317/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_7_Golden_Age__Sydney__image_by_Douglas_Lance_Gibson.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

The Golden Age Cocktail Bar and Cinema in Sydney, Australia. Photo by Douglas Lance Gibson.

## Cairo: Diana Palace Theater

The Diana Palace Theater opened in 1932 as one of Cairo’s most glamorous gathering spots, welcoming the Egyptian elite and, later, weary Allied soldiers during World War II. The Diana is a striking example of Art Deco’s ability to combine the local and global: the facade features Deco details like trapezoidal pavilions and pillars, while Neo-Pharaonic palmettes cling to the building's sides. Having survived a 1952 bombing, the Diana remains one of Cairo’s most beloved movie houses.

## Amsterdam: Tuschinski Theater

Rising over Rembrandt Square in the heart of Amsterdam, the opulent Tuschinski Theater was built from 1918 to 1921 by Jewish developer Abraham Tuschinski. Although he died at the hands of the Nazis during World War II, his movie palace commemorates his vision: the building is flanked by two dome-topped towers, while interiors are filled with gilded geometric lamps accented by carved wood walls, glazed tiles and bronze ornaments; the original stage and Wurlitzer-Strunk organ still stand.

![Image 11: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/4gR7sCCmGAnIPDH6YdQBG0/46e87306840da479786634e4ad2f5453/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_Flickr_Theater_Tuschinski__Amsterdam__image_by_Jennifer_Brandel.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

The Tuschinski Theater in Amsterdam. Photo by Jennifer Brandel.

## London: Rio Cinema

In the trendy Dalston area of East London, the Rio is one of the city’s best-known and beloved movie theaters. It was originally fashioned in 1909 from a converted auctioneers’ shop and was later given the Art Deco facade, with its period-styled signage, that still exists today. Inside the theater, the soaring curved ceilings are accented by Deco-style fluted gold design features. Recently, a second screen was added, which now specializes in independent cinema and film festivals.

![Image 12: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/1QTgEKCoKXgSrd7j9i5ay3/02ea941a508fd28d580ccfe77920bdfa/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_8_Flickr_Rio_Cinema__London.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

The Rio in Dalston, East London.

# Culture

Trends, opinions, and insights from inspiring destinations.

[![Image 2](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/76ysNv97cGTvfjWqYsTRR7/80a3fcaaa9bc2490ca7c3c072a749fd0/8.15.26_Which_Japanese_Island_Are_You_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Japan # Which (Lesser-Known) Japanese Island Are You? Beyond the well-trodden Tokyo–Kyoto corridor, there are thousand-year-old cedar forests, cycling paths through citrus groves, world-class museums reached only by ferry, and some of the country’s most coveted seafood.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/best-japanese-islands-travel [link_4])[![Image 3](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/3XWg3BzzQBAfLrMnTd5Z75/fdb98057266263cbc0e19f1bd73aab7a/8.12.26_LES_Guide_Refresh_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)New York City # LES Is More The Lower East Side is where Hokkaido izakayas, Basque wine bars, and some of New York's best galleries and vintage stores vie for your attention.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/lower-east-side-new-york-guide [link_5])[![Image 4](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/65nO4YGaudogT9oXzWay4R/bfffc5a5126b2306d1a9086f9018c175/7.11.26_-_Mani_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Mani Peninsula # Reaching the End of the Road in Greece On the Mani Peninsula, Monica Mendal traces a path through one-taverna towns, past Byzantine chapels, and down to deserted aquamarine coves at the mainland’s southern tip.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/mani-peninsula-greece-road-trip [link_6])[![Image 5](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/4MBropsx6QLCJ1gJ4QSH1T/3a25e63980c57fbca572259b583870de/Podcast_Recaps_Jenna_Lyons_-_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Global # The True Colors of Jenna Lyons What can a Kyoto broom-maker, a French tart, and a Mongolian cashmere goat teach us about fashion? The designer and former J.Crew creative director has a few ideas.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/traveling-through-jenna-lyons [link_7])[![Image 6](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/72FZvDWQ490ir6POEdw1LA/0476e6ea695a85242cc7f1db94e8c7bd/1.4.25-Antwerp_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Belgium # All About Antwerp Uncovering the subtle swagger of Belgium’s most underrated city through the prism of art, design, and food.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/all-about-antwerp [link_8])[![Image 7](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/5ZlDSVDgF7ELgKskpcAdIv/c6c8b763e1d31de46c40685238dbb339/Podcast_Recaps_David_Remnick-INDEX.jpg?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)New York City # David Remnick Wants You to Stop Collecting Destinations In the second episode of Traveling Through, the longtime New Yorker editor argues that paying attention matters more than passport stamps—and that the best journeys are sometimes on the page.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/traveling-through-david-remnick [link_9])[![Image 8](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/5AeTC1IHTTiBioujihVsGG/df77ef79b1b2c0d10f45b6f9fc6aacf6/Podcast_Recaps_Athena_Calderone-INDEX.jpg?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Global # The Eye(Swoon) Has to Travel In the debut episode of Traveling Through, Athena Calderone reflects on solo journeys, Moroccan riads, Viennese craftsmanship, and how curiosity became her greatest teacher.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/traveling-through-athena-calderone [link_10])[![Image 9](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/kg3Oa8jorC1ZXU7cMZsbG/51143a678842c1de8265ecb11b9f483e/6.6.26_Malta_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Malta # It’s Malta’s Moment A fresco-filled hotel in a limestone mansion, a resurgence of local craft, and a new nonstop flight are putting wind in Malta’s sails. Here’s how to experience the island right now.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/malta-travel-guide [link_11])[![Image 10](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/N80kK05JKLJTUfl5NOlqL/a89fc454b0f4e095e698429f290d1d7f/5.16.25_Hyeres_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)South of France # A Rare Quiet Corner of the French Riviera In Hyères, newly revived seaside hotels sit beside Romanesque churches, flamingo-filled salt marshes, and stretches of scrubby coastline.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/hyeres-france-travel-guide [link_12])[![Image 11](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/2RqrwyEmGymjaYFtULhLMM/5fd38c4294ef9ef2f634a1a34c794bab/5.16.26_Flamenco_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Andalusia # Flamenco Won’t Stand Still From its roots in Romani communities to Rosalía’s ‘Lux’ megatour, a musical form born on the fringes keeps evolving—without losing its edge.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/flamenco-from-andalusia-to-rosalia [link_13])[![Image 12](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/7aiuih9cDcRreYunAPjelT/b54fec2f1d62228bb7ad513524bdea5a/4.25.26_Eternal_Summer_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Global # A Time and a Place With a bit of foresight, you can embark on 12 months of travel timed for gentle sunlight, long days, and destinations at their fullest expression.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/where-to-go-each-month-travel-guide [link_14])[![Image 13](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/6Htrx5SnALntGHOD9Xhw8J/b4ea762a35244d0b8daa7e834f8f5aa5/4.18.26_Greece_Photo_Essay_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Cyclades # Beyond Santorini: Summer in Sifnos, Therasia, and Folegandros Wind-whipped scrub, volcanic vineyards, and hidden coves show each Aegean landscape at its most elemental.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/travel-cyclades-sifnos-folegandros-thirassia-guide [link_15])[![Image 14](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/3GDdxTAHwrYLPDZV0MlnPP/8425287d6c6bb5a070a3bb99853b2bd4/3.21.26_Fez_Guide_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Fez # Fez, Inside and Out Morocco’s ancient capital is undergoing a cultural revival—but its souks, crafts, and majestic architecture are as compelling as ever.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/fez-morocco-travel-guide [link_16])[![Image 15](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/395WlonK434Qqntp2IaU85/a507a5ea2c23c83aa8180dc4e7a54d73/3.7.26_Carabanchel_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Madrid # The Other Madrid South of the river, beyond the postcard center, Carabanchel is where the city still feels like itself—and where its creative pulse beats strongest.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/carabanchel-madrid-creative-district [link_17])[![Image 16](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/4tKeW73JlU1tvxipXBDkYi/63afe7db4660ec6b0c81706a944099bf/3.4.26_Japan_Inside_The_Itinerary_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Japan # Inside the Itinerary: The Culinary Heritage of Japan An inside look at our group journey across Japan, from knife forging in Sakai to Buddhist cuisine in a private temple to 72 seasons of seafood.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/inside-itinerary-japan-2026 [link_18])[![Image 17](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/4VlQJQhq7K0G4wLEmzZM6c/dbfa469529579118a3a62d85814c36c9/2.14.25_Wuthering_Heights_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Yorkshire # The Landscape That Made ‘Wuthering Heights’ The moors, manor houses, and ruins of Yorkshire still conjure Brontë’s haunting, brutally romantic world.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/bronte-wuthering-heights-yorkshire [link_19])[![Image 18](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/58pBuQw21WJV5fq20AhuSL/947f5e19e5d56932e23d717be53b930b/12.27.25_Travel_Moments_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Global # The 2025 Travel Moments We’ll Remember From pilgrimages to Armenian monasteries to samba-filled festas in Brazil and meditating in Menorca’s premier art space, these trips left a mark on our team.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/2025-travel-moments-well-remember [link_20])[![Image 19](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/3ecK6XdWRqIcOfN31aKdK/5dc2edfec16a52d0e197b5a2f20b8b2c/12.20.25_Northern_Territory_Australia_INDEX.png?w=512&fm=webp&q=75)Northern Territories # Australia’s New Creative Frontier In Darwin, Arnhem Land, and the Tiwi Islands, an electrifying music and arts scene is rewarding travelers who make the journey north.](https://priorworld.com/editorial/australia-new-creative-frontier [link_21])

## A Spanish Seafood Pilgrimage

Along Spain’s northern coast, where percebes and anchovies are a near revelation, the Atlantic speaks through fishermen’s stews, simply prepared shellfish, and open-fire meals rooted in tradition. From the Camino’s misty trails to cider-soaked Asturias and the culinary heartland of the Basque Country, this is a journey shaped by tide, flame, and centuries of seafaring culture.

# Our Tbilisi Black Book

The author of _Georgia: The Cookbook_ shares his favorite addresses for holy-grail khachapuri, surprising Soviet antiques, and clay-aged wine poured well past 2 a.m.

![Image 2](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/5p2jjXWQ43Zr8RM7vmjFW6/dc981076d236285560afc1e5d288b807/10.3.26_Tbilisi_HERO.png?w=2400&fm=webp&q=75)

Category:[Culture](https://priorworld.com/editorial/categories/culture)

Words by:

[Benjamin Kemper](https://priorworld.com/author/benjamin-kemper)

Published October 2, 2026

Last month, as pedestrians grumbled about roadworks on Tbilisi’s main thoroughfare, construction workers’ shovels clinked against something astonishing: a [trove](https://www.reuters.com/science/roadworks-georgias-capital-uncover-rare-10th-century-pottery-cache-2026-09-09/) of intricate pottery from roughly the 10th century, when the city was still heaving with Silk Road caravanserais and floating flour mills bobbed on the Mtkvari River. The find barely registered to most Georgians: In a country that claims an 8,000-year-old winemaking tradition, the [earliest known](https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5225/) hominin remains outside Africa, and churches dating back to the 4th century, a millennium-old cache is just another day in the Georgian capital.

If, like me, you love sprawling, palimpsest-like cities where centuries of history pig-pile on one another, there are few places more thrilling than Tbilisi. That’s why I’ve taken more than 25 trips there over the last decade—and why it inspired my new [Georgian cookbook](https://publishing.hardiegrant.com/en-au/books/georgia-by-meriko-gubeladze/9781958417898), coauthored with chef Meriko Gubeladze (more on her shortly).

![Image 3](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/Vxt78KtMtaMpBQuXdF3B8/d84a94ee2ff0329c2cd27d57e4afc9bc/Spain_2027_web_Gallery-9.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## PRIOR Access: a dedicated Travel Designer and unlimited trip planning for $3,250 a year, with the same network of insiders behind our stories.

[LEARN MORE](https://priorworld.com/travel-design)

But despite Tbilisi’s sudden rise to the top of travel wishlists—its airport handled a record 4.75 million passengers in 2024, nearly 30 percent more than the year prior—I’ve seen surprisingly little change in the standard itinerary over the years. Most visitors seem to ride the cable car up to the fortress, post a few stories in the Old Town, nab a Soviet something-or-other at the flea market, then skedaddle to the mountains. There’s nothing wrong with that cookie-cutter tour—it’s hard to leave Tbilisi anything but spellbound—but having nearly moved there, beguiled by its layered peculiarity, I can assure you: The city rewards straying mightily.

My favorite addresses run the gamut: there's the back-alley lunch joint serving spicy $4 stews, the natural wine bar tended by friends who are actual winemakers, and the buzzy new boutique where couture hounds drop stacks of Georgian lari on Galliano’s Dior and ’80s Lacroix. Consider this your invitation to dig a little deeper.

![Image 4](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/3j5o5QvSBjF2UXXYAWUOq9/748a0ec3eeded430625035eeea23e9ec/10.3.26_Tbilisi_body_1A.png?w=2400&fm=webp&q=75)

![Image 5](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/67ajfC5tqOaDQGfvTcFpjO/059e93dd974fa1c754718be466846418/10.3.26_Tbilisi_body_1B.png?w=2400&fm=webp&q=75)

![Image 6](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/45uDjCPpOZQiQoNKElq19Y/933ad9982a22ce88b759b326c7062d5a/10.3.26_Tbilisi_body_1C.png?w=2400&fm=webp&q=75)

![Image 7](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/5BjwwLJm9FCZObkH4NS1SD/66f09316a2d3e09cddf3d74e3582f070/10.3.26_Tbilisi_body_1D.png?w=2400&fm=webp&q=75)

## The pied-à-terre: Stamba Hotel

_14 Merab Kostava St._

Where would Tbilisi be without [Stamba Hotel](https://stambahotel.com/) and its Adjara Group brethren ([Fabrika](https://fabrikatbilisi.com/) and [Rooms](https://roomshotels.com/hotel/tbilisi/))? It certainly wouldn’t be topping lists of the trendiest cities on earth. Stamba is one of my favorite hotels anywhere, in part because it’s aesthetically unplaceable: Look one way and you’ll see thickets of cacti; look another and there are supple, snaking leather sofas; look up and ceiling-mounted machinery that once shuttled papers along a conveyor belt still looms overhead, a reminder of the building’s origins as a Soviet printing house. If you stay here, book an Aviator room, outfitted with a freestanding brass tub, a La Marzocco espresso machine, and a McIntosh stereo system.

But what puts Stamba in an echelon all its own is its self-contained cultural ecosystem that locals enjoy as much as guests. You could happily spend a whole day here, and I occasionally do, swanning from the café with its house-roasted beans to the Japanese-ish teriyaki joint to Warehouse, my beloved nook for deep-cut natural wines. Somewhere in there, I’ll inevitably wind up at the white-tablecloth restaurant for an Adjaruli khachapuri, that molten cheesy canoe topped with egg yolk and butter that you gloop together with a spoon. Come sundown, everyone spills into the enormous courtyard out back, which swells into a wine-sloshed scene.

![Image 8: The pied-à-terre: Stamba Hotel](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/5hjdg48wuSu0yjKQoiDAdt/fb75a0b571f76e14dd2a6154842f5844/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Stamba_Hotel.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## Holy-grail Imeruli khachapuri: Shavi Lomi

_30 Zurab Kvlividze St._

[Shavi Lomi](https://www.instagram.com/shavilomi_tbilisicuisine/?hl=es) occupies a creaky old house filled with patterned tablecloths, cats flitting between tables, and the buttery glow of antique light fixtures. In an era of “concept” restaurants, Shavi Lomi is refreshingly analog: It’s about providing comfort, nourishment, and maybe even a sense of homecoming.

Chef Meriko Gubeladze, the owner and my cookbook coauthor, is something of a household name in Georgia: She hosted a primetime cooking show for a decade and cooked for Anthony Bourdain when _Parts Unknown_ came to Tbilisi. Originally from Imereti, she makes the finest version I’ve tried of her region’s namesake khachapuri: a dinner plate-size, double-crusted pie filled with tangy, curdy cheese. It’s soft, foldy, and not too doughy—perfect alongside Gurian black tea at breakfast or dipped into tkemali (sour plum sauce) for a snack.

![Image 9: Holy-grail Imeruli khachapuri: Shavi Lomi](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/5x88OZSpXUqgEqRhgypFGF/dcc2121a136228a93255fc38fb1ce871/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Shavi_Lomi.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## Surprising Soviet crafts: Navtlughi Market

_Mevele Dead End_

Dry Bridge flea market is Tbilisi’s legendary antiquing stop, but in recent years, the quality has slipped, and there’s a nagging sense that you’re often picking through the dregs. Not so at Navtlughi, a ramshackle maze of sheds and market stalls on the fringes of town where you can shop for traditional hand-whittled mtsvadi (kebab) skewers, Caucasian rugs woven deep in the mountains on long-retired looms, beeswax candles made by monks, and enough bric-à-brac to make a packrat short-circuit. On a recent visit, I was hellbent on finding a Soviet gluggle and matching shot-glass set. Manufactured mostly in Ukraine and gilded by hand, these fish pitchers with gaping maws are hilarious to look at—and increasingly scarce. With one of these on the table, there’s no better way to wrangle your friends into a round of chacha, Georgia’s fiery grape brandy.

![Image 10: Surprising Soviet crafts: Navtlughi Market](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/3yfI8PP0pFbQW8Hg32pMZ1/6cc940f9657c382f059c2063ed4388bc/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Navtlughi_Market.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The fashion fix: Archived Couture

_12 Leo Kiacheli St._

Eight years ago, Luka Gviniashvili started amassing what has become perhaps the world’s largest private collection of Christian Lacroix, and today it’s on display at his three-year-old boutique, [Archive Couture](https://archivedcouture.com/). The space was conceived with Lacroix himself and channels his gloriously OTT ’80s salons with lipstick-red floors and black ornamental flourishes. The collection is just as exuberant, mixing Lacroix haute couture and ready-to-wear with 20th-century fashion, jewelry, historical textiles, and even liturgical vestments. It’s technically an archive, but don’t expect white gloves and hushed voices: You can wander in off the street, get up close to the clothes, and, crucially, buy whatever you see.

![Image 11: The fashion fix: Archived Couture](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/2Bs70WC5czEGoa7A9mIwsj/c221eb833ef9083248df08cd2312bd96/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Archived_Couture.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The edible haul: Dezerter’s Bazaar

_5 Abastumani St._

One of Georgia's most eye-catching foods is churchkhela, a knobbly confection made by dipping strings of nuts (usually walnuts, sometimes hazelnuts) repeatedly into thickened, sweetened grape juice. It’s something of a primordial power bar: Georgian soldiers are said to have loaded their saddlebags with them before heading into battle. Today you can buy churchkhela just about everywhere for your own road trips and cheese boards, but the best are handmade and sold at markets like Dezerter's Bazaar. Look for pale brownish-pink ones that still bend slightly in the middle, and avoid anything stiff, cracked, or artificially colored. While you’re at the bazaar, stock up on Georgia’s holy trinity of spices: coriander, dried marigold, and blue fenugreek. To find my spice angel, Shazina, amid the throngs, simply ask a friendly (ideally non-spice) vendor to point you in the direction of Shazina, “the spice lady.”

![Image 12: The edible haul: Dezerter’s Bazaar](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/6Bb1UxFTkQXiua3tBui0f5/3c61a17e7da89799c036d68af0dfeaed/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Spices_from_Dezerters_Bazaar.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The unsung cultural stop: Silk Museum

_6 Giorgi Tsabadze St._

Tbilisi’s [State Silk Museum](https://silkmuseum.ge/) celebrates the strange alchemy of turning silkworm spit into finery. Silk was once serious business in Georgia: Mulberry trees grew across the country to feed armies of ravenous silkworms, whose cocoons supplied a thriving local industry. Founded in the late 19th century as part of the Caucasian Sericulture Station, the museum gets wonderfully granular about the whole process, with cocoons, antique looms, shimmering textiles, and other silky arcana. After a respectful four-year restoration, it reopened in 2024 to little fanfare, still decked out with its original display cases, patterned floors, and intricately carved woodwork. Even if you’re not obsessed with silk, the redbrick building alone is worth the detour.

![Image 13: The unsung cultural stop: Silk Museum](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/2pGSFpWxY9P2G6sjw19CPz/5c2651c6459d55e60c711ee47090db89/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Silk_Museum.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## My architectural crush: Bank of Georgia Headquarters

_29a Iuri Gagarini St._

The Bank of Georgia headquarters is a hulking Jenga tower of concrete slabs cantilevered over a wooded slope above the Mtkvari. To this day, every time I drive past it on the highway, I crane my neck out the window to get a better look. Built in 1975 as the headquarters of the Georgian SSR’s Ministry of Highway Construction, it’s a Soviet Brutalist triumph that looks as though half of it is floating in midair.

But since it’s hard to visit in person, I’ll send you instead to the Persian Mirror Halls at the Tbilisi State Academy of Arts, where, inside a 19th-century mansion, you’ll find fairytale rooms encrusted with Qajar-style mirrorwork. Installed by Persian craftsmen, the tiny shards of glass tessellate the walls and ceilings alongside painted flowers and nature motifs; stained-glass windows throw colored light across the whole confection. It’s a wondrous bit of Tehran hiding in central Tbilisi.

![Image 14: My architectural crush: Bank of Georgia Headquarters](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/6m4PT1CGNNxjoGxdrvaClg/4ae8ff2477ace6962d56191cf9dad6da/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Bank_of_Georgia_Headquarters.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The daytime hangout: Honoré

_4 Constitution St._

[Honoré](https://www.instagram.com/honore.tbilisi/?hl=es) occupies an old building whose renovation left its bones on full display: Soaring gallery windows and battered columns contrast with a wraparound cocktail bar, a killer sound system, and a garden with picnic tables where you can watch mtsvadi sputter over the coals. I like it best during the day, when things are quiet enough to post up by the windows and watch cats wander in from the garden and toast themselves on the radiators. I’ll often sit for hours, starting with lunch—always the (unfortunately named) “bean plate,” a heap of spicy beans with sharp Guda cheese and a whole cucumber thwacked open and salted—then move on to coffee, maybe dessert, then another coffee, working or reading all the while.

![Image 15: The daytime hangout: Honoré](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/7pITkDZQXL66m9APWSg05V/3dbaabb60910f2b028eaf8905576d69d/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Honore.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The scavenger hunt: Tbilisi Gold Market

_Tbilisi Central Station_

The Tbilisi Gold Market packs some of the city’s most precious specimens into an unlikely setting: the ground floor of a gritty train station, a late-Soviet concrete pile with a space-age sweep to its facade. Inside, the sheer volume of tchotchkes can scramble your brain, so go with at least a vague idea of what you’re hunting for, whether it’s a gold bracelet, a Soviet watch, or an antique niello-silver cigarette case. It’s worth haggling until the cows come home, and if you’re buying actual gold, have the piece tested before you pay: There’s a lab at the back of the market that offers a free service.

![Image 16: The scavenger hunt: Tbilisi Gold Market](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/5rjeJzLvCKnNigyYiN8OEB/1e96680ce7c2a4df06395d24381d3e02/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Gold_Market.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The dinner spot: Ninia’s Garden

_97 Dimitri Uznadze St._

If Shavi Lomi is Gubeladze in grandmotherly mode—all snug rooms and lovingly prepared Georgian staples—[Ninia’s Garden](https://www.instagram.com/ninias_garden/?hl=en) is where she lets her creativity fully unspool. A tomato salad comes with hunks of sourdough made from doli, a salvaged ancient Georgian red wheat; ajapsandali, the normally ratatouille-like combination of eggplant, peppers, and tomato, goes from amorphous to geometrical with crisp batons of fried eggplant; and a waffle arrives under yogurt cream and glossy beet confit. The cooking is playful, but never so cheffy that you lose sight of what you’re eating.

![Image 17: The dinner spot: Ninia’s Garden](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/YlvwldBwpAfWUKO6BFhwF/93c13effbf156b244fb97a6fd110741e/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Ninias_Garden.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The side quest: Chronicle of Georgia

_Chronicle of Georgia_

Started in 1985 by Georgian sculptor Zurab Tsereteli, the Chronicle of Georgia was built to memorialize the nation’s history, with 16 colossal pillars depicting Georgian royalty and epic battles interspersed with scenes from the life of Christ. It was never completed, which explains the blank panels and bare concrete. Wandering between its 100-foot-tall bronze figures is like stumbling into some ancient fantastical kingdom where a pterodactyl could swoop down at any moment.

![Image 18: The side quest: Chronicle of Georgia](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/7x2VCpEUj69zCsG5H2JKb6/da3c28fa5337dbbd9e8c174b927a952a/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Chronicle_of_Georgia.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The culinary deep cut: Pingvinebi

_Zhiuli Shartava Street_

I only found Pingvinebi because a friend tipped me off, and even after decades in business, most Tbilisians have no idea it exists. The no-frills room has tiled floors, a jukebox jerry-rigged to staticky speakers, tables of men clacking backgammon pieces and swigging Kazbegi beer, and prices that remind me of when I first came to Georgia, when almost nothing cost more than a few bucks.

God only knows why it’s called “Penguins,” a theme carried through with stuffed penguins and paintings on the walls. Order the spicy, tomatoey “soup” kharcho and katleti (pan-fried beef patties) with mashed potatoes, then peek into the kitchen, where women in splotched aprons stir enormous pots of stews in varying shades of orange, red, and brown. Nobody speaks much English, so this is where Google Translate comes in handy; it’s cash only, too.

# LES Is More

The Lower East Side is where Hokkaido izakayas, Basque wine bars, and some of New York's best galleries and vintage stores vie for your attention.

![Image 2](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/52ojY3IkA0q5fT84zS50I1/d6b9db99a2fc69248d21cb3520e1be01/8.12.26_LES_Guide_Refresh_HERO.png?w=2400&fm=webp&q=75)

Category:[Culture](https://priorworld.com/editorial/categories/culture)

Words by:

[Patrick McGraw](https://priorworld.com/author/patrick-mcgraw)

Published July 8, 2022

Updated August 12, 2026

Manhattan’s neighborhoods have always resisted neat boundaries, but few are as expansive—or as shape-shifting—as the Lower East Side. These days, its influence spills beyond its traditional borders, bleeding into neighboring enclaves like Chinatown and Little Italy. Cracking downtown’s ever-evolving codes can feel daunting, but whether you come for the restaurants, the independent shops, or a new generation of galleries, you’ll find a neighborhood in its prime.

The “LES” has changed significantly since its heyday in the ’70s and ’80s, when the area attracted a mix of students, musicians, and immigrants from Bangladesh, China, the Dominican Republic, and Poland. Those pre-gentrification glory days may have cemented its status as a global emblem of cool, but that kind of scrappiness can feel elusive amid New York’s increasingly polished landscape. Even so, the Lower East Side has resisted becoming fully sanitized thanks to its freewheeling mix of subcultures old and new.

In recent years, a small slice of the Lower East Side known colloquially as Dimes Square—named after Dimes, the buzzy restaurant as famous for its matcha buttermilk pancakes as its good-looking waiters—has become the neighborhood’s epicenter of art, food, fashion, and media gossip. High-profile openings like the Nine Orchard hotel, housed in a meticulously restored Beaux-Arts landmark a stone’s throw from the East Broadway subway stop, have only accelerated the area’s gilded makeover. By design, however, the Lower East Side is still hard to define in broad brushstrokes. The dress code is at once minimal and over-the-top; the attitude both laid-back—almost to the point of aloofness—and brimming with youthful energy.

In many ways, traversing the Lower East Side feels like watching the hodgepodge freneticism of the internet spring to life, where tastes and aesthetics mutate almost as quickly as the latest TikTok meme. Yet for all its “very online” energy, the neighborhood remains firmly rooted in its immigrant and artistic past. Here, PRIOR rounds up the galleries, hotels, boutiques, and restaurants that best reflect the Lower East Side’s forever-restless soul.

### [Nine Orchard](https://nineorchard.com/)

_9 Orchard Street_  
_212-804-9900_

The Beaux-Arts landmark that was once a bank is now a swanky 116-room hotel with a bistro, lounge, and, come September, a 44-seat fine-dining restaurant from Ignacio Mattos, the chef behind Estela and Altro Paradiso. Though the building has been extensively restored, it has kept plenty of nods to its gilded past. Archival photographs served as the blueprint for reconstructing its original clock and 60-foot rooftop cupola, while the former bank teller hall, with its soaring ceilings and arched windows, has been transformed into The Lobby Lounge, where Dimes Square regulars sip martinis amid old-world ornamentation.

# Dine

### [Dr Clark](https://www.drclarkhouse.com/)

_104 Bayard Street_  
_917-426-4454_

Across the street from Columbus Park and the looming Lower Manhattan Criminal Courts, Dr. Clark bills itself as New York City’s first Hokkaido bar—a Japanese restaurant and karaoke spot rolled into one. The menu ranges from pristine sashimi to grilled lamb, best enjoyed in a warmly lit, wood-clad interior by Green River Project, the design studio behind the Bode Tailor Shop and the neighboring Bode-owned River bar.

### [Elbow Bread](https://www.elbowbread.shop/)

_1 Ludlow Street_  
_212-837-2963_

Come early if you want the full selection at Elbow Bread, the small-batch bakery that has quickly become one of the neighborhood’s essential stops, thanks to pastries like the strawberry, lemon, and sheep’s cheese Danish, excellent bialys, and a rotating lineup of weekend doughnuts.

### Ha’s Snack Bar

_297 Broome Street_

Opened in 2025 by Sadie Mae Burns-Ha and Anthony Ha, Ha’s Snack Bar packs outsize ambition into a tiny dining room. Following the success of [Ha’s Đặc Biệt](https://www.instagram.com/has_dac_biet/?hl=es) and Bistro Ha, the couple’s latest restaurant is currently one of the Lower East Side’s toughest tables, with nightly lines meandering down the sidewalk. The menu draws heavily on Anthony Ha’s Vietnamese heritage but isn’t inhibited by it, pairing dishes like pâté chaud—flaky pastry stuffed with ground pork, mushrooms, and vermicelli—with tamarind-glazed snails and other playful forays into international cuisines.

### [Dhamaka](https://www.dhamaka.nyc/)

_119 Delancey Street_

Downtown sensation Dhamaka hasn’t lost an ounce of hype since it first opened in a corner of Essex Street Market in 2021. Run by chef Chintan Pandya and restaurateur Roni Mazumdar, the menu aims to highlight “forgotten” Indian dishes rather than committing to a specific regional cuisine. It’s known for adventurous plates like goat neck, kidneys, bone marrow, and the Rajasthani khargosh—a slow-roasted rabbit feast that must be requested days in advance and has been billed as New York’s most impossible-to-order dish.

# Cinemas Paradiso

A number of the world’s most glamorous Art Deco theaters remain emblems of our cinematic dreams

![Image 2](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/7Cy6S1GeB8W16reFdft0z8/b32e167a6938edbc6f2f890f5799a738/Hero_Opener_3.5.21_2.png?w=2400&fm=webp&q=75)

Category:[Culture](https://priorworld.com/editorial/categories/culture)

Location:[Egypt](https://priorworld.com/destinations/egypt)

Words by:

[PRIOR Team](https://priorworld.com/author/prior-team)

Photography:Angela Witmore

Published March 5, 2021

Few existing architectural symbols capture the boom of Hollywood’s nascent cinema industry more evocatively than Art Deco theaters. These emerged in the 1920s and ‘30s as Art Deco and Art Nouveau were reaching their zeniths, but also in the midst of other historic milestones: the Flapper Era, the Suffragist Movement, Paris’ ascent on the global artistic stage and, of course, the Great Depression. With their facades boldly festooned in heraldic chevrons and courtly colonnades, Art Deco theaters across the globe stood as symbols of the interwar era’s cultural and commercial optimism.

Often seating thousands, these temples of high and pop culture emerged as essential gathering spots for the urban affluent and entertainment-hungry masses. They also often contained technological wonders like air-conditioning, elevators and parking, still rarities at the time. These cultural centers offered the public an escape from the urban chaos to lose themselves in the grandeur and romance that only Hollywood can deliver—all accented by the Deco era’s futuristic splendor.

![Image 3: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/5m7ZdbvJipfgA3KdDxbcbz/b526e16c6f7a763112847e11a5d27928/Content_Portrait_Intro_Cinema_Rif_in_Tangiers__image_by_Conor_Burke.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

Inside Cinéma Rif in Tangier, Morocco. Photo by Conor Burke.

Many of the most elaborate of these Art Deco gems have been destroyed or repurposed—the Odeon Marble Arch in London was demolished in 1964 to make way for a widescreen cinema, while the curvilinear Alhambra in Tel Aviv is now consecrated to another Hollywood fixation as a Church of Scientology center. But many still stand strong—some even continuing to show films, others now used as performance halls. Whatever their contemporary function, these enduring beauties are still worth a visit to take in their mix of Art Deco flavor meshed with local culture and materials. Here are a few worth flying for.

## Los Angeles: Grauman’s Egyptian Theatre

No cinema better evokes Hollywood’s Deco-era lore like the Grauman’s Egyptian Theatre in Los Angeles. Built in downtown L.A. in 1928, it was designed in a Deco-meets-Pharaonic style now known as Neo-Egyptian, with hieroglyphs inside and out, along with four massive columns fronting the theater’s main entrance—each more than 20 feet wide. Home to the first-ever movie premiere (_Robin Hood_ in 1922), it’s now owned, of course, by Netflix, which intends to use the space for special film events.

![Image 4: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/3PxCoXNhGhW1odS3AGObuY/c92e523b9cd2883734b1f4bebeadd3fa/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_Intro_2_Wikipedia_Egyptian_Theater__Los_Angeles.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

The Grauman’s Egyptian Theatre in Los Angeles.

## Mexico City: Cine Metropólitan

In the historic Centro district, the 1943 Cine Metropólitan—which originally held 3,600 seats—is fittingly grand for a city of 20 million. It debuted as a movie theater with a linear Art Deco facade by Mexican architect Pedro Gorozpe; interiors are French neoclassical, with gilded corinthian columns and oil paintings depicting aristocratic life. In the ‘50s, it became _the_ place for children in Mexico City to watch Disney movies; today it’s a concert venue known as the Teatro Metropolitan.

![Image 5: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/1Z4kECVpQO0MryUNa16xGp/3e9923803c0c40b93b6edb0a263656a4/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_2_Wikipedia_Metropolitan__Mexico_City.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

Cine Metropólitan in Mexico City.

## Oakland, CA: The Paramount

The 1931 Paramount Theater stands as a symbol of its own glory, having once prevailed as the Bay Area’s most influential cinema. Built by Timothy Pflueger, the San Francisco architect behind the city’s Pacific Coast Stock Exchange, the Paramount was acquired by the City of Oakland, which oversaw a meticulous restoration that preserved most of its Deco details—zig-zagged flooring and swirling ceiling lights. Today it hosts a robust film schedule and is home to the Oakland Symphony Orchestra.

![Image 6: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/5j7drdxzzmXlyP5HoPiq6I/3ec61757bd99751f1dd4ae46e5e3b590/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_3_Wikipedia_Paramount__Oakland__CA.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

The Paramount in Oakland, California.

## Istanbul: Süreyya Opera House

Set in Istanbul’s upscale Kadıköy district near the Bosphorus, the 1920s-era Süreyya is distinguished by its carved-stone facade evoking European Belle-Epoque designs. The interiors are Art Deco dreamscapes, with richly-inlaid ceiling murals, curved balustrades and Tiffany-style chandeliers. Though the Süreyya was envisioned as a place for opera and musical theater, it had a colorful history as a site for weddings, plays and a cinema; today, the Istanbul State Opera and Ballet commands the stage.

![Image 7: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/4Oc3gBUFFbepg7wJNeggfS/4032714bd4a31efb8ca24fc1578e144c/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_4_Flickr_Su__reyya_Opera_House.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

Süreyya Opera House in Istanbul, Turkey.

## Mumbai: The Regal

In the 1930s, when Mumbai rose as India’s answer to Hollywood, the Regal was the city’s most glorious Art Deco cinema. It debuted in 1933 on the busy Colaba Causeway, and, according to lore, was India’s first fully air-conditioned theater. The Regal’s concrete exterior is topped by a ziggurat-style crown; interiors are lined in elaborate Czech mirrors, orange and jade-green sunray motifs and _bas_-relief theatrical masks flanking the massive movie screen, which still regularly shows films.

![Image 8: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/5rKii54zuEywdpD57XtQBb/32c17b3645c331f2dbfeaa5974fbf67d/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_5_Flickr_Regal_Mumbai__image_by_Gioconda_Beekman.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

The Regal in Mumbai. Photo by Gioconda Beekman.

## Casablanca: Cinema Rialto

During the early 20th-century French Protectorate era, shining examples of Art Deco proliferated across Morocco, among them the lattice-fronted Cinema Rif in Tangier. In Casablanca, the 1929 Cinema Rialto is also an Art Deco icon, its name prominently etched on a swish red-and-ochre facade and its roof capped by a cupola. With a single screen facing 1,350 plush red seats, the Rialto was always (and still is) a movie theater, but has also welcomed the likes of performers Edith Piaf and Josephine Baker.

![Image 9: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/3eewrk2mkXNS4xVSK9i1kR/4c520a74caa7384399fed216b811d298/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_6_Flickr_Rialto__Casablanca__image_by_Jean-Franc__ois_Gornet.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

Cinema Rialto in Casablanca, Morocco. Photo by Jean-François Gornet.

## Sydney: Golden Age Cinema

The Golden Age Cocktail Bar and Cinema may now be a place where you can catch a classic film while enjoying a craft cocktail, but it began life as the Deco-divine home of Paramount Pictures in Australia. Completed in 1940, the building—set in the affluent Surrey Hills district—was both a film house and office block, all devoted to movies. Paramount House has been thoroughly updated, though it retains its elegant brass windows, cut-glass chandeliers and its streamlined, nautical-inspired facade.

![Image 10: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/4h1TkULZc29moY6k0fbZlH/69941404734cc450533a6da3d929c317/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_7_Golden_Age__Sydney__image_by_Douglas_Lance_Gibson.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

The Golden Age Cocktail Bar and Cinema in Sydney, Australia. Photo by Douglas Lance Gibson.

## Cairo: Diana Palace Theater

The Diana Palace Theater opened in 1932 as one of Cairo’s most glamorous gathering spots, welcoming the Egyptian elite and, later, weary Allied soldiers during World War II. The Diana is a striking example of Art Deco’s ability to combine the local and global: the facade features Deco details like trapezoidal pavilions and pillars, while Neo-Pharaonic palmettes cling to the building's sides. Having survived a 1952 bombing, the Diana remains one of Cairo’s most beloved movie houses.

## Amsterdam: Tuschinski Theater

Rising over Rembrandt Square in the heart of Amsterdam, the opulent Tuschinski Theater was built from 1918 to 1921 by Jewish developer Abraham Tuschinski. Although he died at the hands of the Nazis during World War II, his movie palace commemorates his vision: the building is flanked by two dome-topped towers, while interiors are filled with gilded geometric lamps accented by carved wood walls, glazed tiles and bronze ornaments; the original stage and Wurlitzer-Strunk organ still stand.

![Image 11: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/4gR7sCCmGAnIPDH6YdQBG0/46e87306840da479786634e4ad2f5453/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_Flickr_Theater_Tuschinski__Amsterdam__image_by_Jennifer_Brandel.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

The Tuschinski Theater in Amsterdam. Photo by Jennifer Brandel.

## London: Rio Cinema

In the trendy Dalston area of East London, the Rio is one of the city’s best-known and beloved movie theaters. It was originally fashioned in 1909 from a converted auctioneers’ shop and was later given the Art Deco facade, with its period-styled signage, that still exists today. Inside the theater, the soaring curved ceilings are accented by Deco-style fluted gold design features. Recently, a second screen was added, which now specializes in independent cinema and film festivals.

![Image 12: Article image](https://images.ctfassets.net/oc8dxvhvd87u/1QTgEKCoKXgSrd7j9i5ay3/02ea941a508fd28d580ccfe77920bdfa/Content_Portrait_3.5.21_8_Flickr_Rio_Cinema__London.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

The Rio in Dalston, East London.
