# Our Tbilisi Black Book

The author of _Georgia: The Cookbook_ shares his favorite addresses for holy-grail khachapuri, surprising Soviet antiques, and clay-aged wine poured well past 2 a.m.

![Image 2](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/5p2jjXWQ43Zr8RM7vmjFW6/dc981076d236285560afc1e5d288b807/10.3.26_Tbilisi_HERO.png?w=2400&fm=webp&q=75)

Category:[Culture](https://priorworld.com/editorial/categories/culture)

Words by:

[Benjamin Kemper](https://priorworld.com/author/benjamin-kemper)

Published October 2, 2026

Last month, as pedestrians grumbled about roadworks on Tbilisi’s main thoroughfare, construction workers’ shovels clinked against something astonishing: a [trove](https://www.reuters.com/science/roadworks-georgias-capital-uncover-rare-10th-century-pottery-cache-2026-09-09/) of intricate pottery from roughly the 10th century, when the city was still heaving with Silk Road caravanserais and floating flour mills bobbed on the Mtkvari River. The find barely registered to most Georgians: In a country that claims an 8,000-year-old winemaking tradition, the [earliest known](https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5225/) hominin remains outside Africa, and churches dating back to the 4th century, a millennium-old cache is just another day in the Georgian capital.

If, like me, you love sprawling, palimpsest-like cities where centuries of history pig-pile on one another, there are few places more thrilling than Tbilisi. That’s why I’ve taken more than 25 trips there over the last decade—and why it inspired my new [Georgian cookbook](https://publishing.hardiegrant.com/en-au/books/georgia-by-meriko-gubeladze/9781958417898), coauthored with chef Meriko Gubeladze (more on her shortly).

![Image 3](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/Vxt78KtMtaMpBQuXdF3B8/d84a94ee2ff0329c2cd27d57e4afc9bc/Spain_2027_web_Gallery-9.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## PRIOR Access: a dedicated Travel Designer and unlimited trip planning for $3,250 a year, with the same network of insiders behind our stories.

[LEARN MORE](https://priorworld.com/travel-design)

But despite Tbilisi’s sudden rise to the top of travel wishlists—its airport handled a record 4.75 million passengers in 2024, nearly 30 percent more than the year prior—I’ve seen surprisingly little change in the standard itinerary over the years. Most visitors seem to ride the cable car up to the fortress, post a few stories in the Old Town, nab a Soviet something-or-other at the flea market, then skedaddle to the mountains. There’s nothing wrong with that cookie-cutter tour—it’s hard to leave Tbilisi anything but spellbound—but having nearly moved there, beguiled by its layered peculiarity, I can assure you: The city rewards straying mightily.

My favorite addresses run the gamut: there's the back-alley lunch joint serving spicy $4 stews, the natural wine bar tended by friends who are actual winemakers, and the buzzy new boutique where couture hounds drop stacks of Georgian lari on Galliano’s Dior and ’80s Lacroix. Consider this your invitation to dig a little deeper.

![Image 4](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/3j5o5QvSBjF2UXXYAWUOq9/748a0ec3eeded430625035eeea23e9ec/10.3.26_Tbilisi_body_1A.png?w=2400&fm=webp&q=75)

![Image 5](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/67ajfC5tqOaDQGfvTcFpjO/059e93dd974fa1c754718be466846418/10.3.26_Tbilisi_body_1B.png?w=2400&fm=webp&q=75)

![Image 6](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/45uDjCPpOZQiQoNKElq19Y/933ad9982a22ce88b759b326c7062d5a/10.3.26_Tbilisi_body_1C.png?w=2400&fm=webp&q=75)

![Image 7](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/5BjwwLJm9FCZObkH4NS1SD/66f09316a2d3e09cddf3d74e3582f070/10.3.26_Tbilisi_body_1D.png?w=2400&fm=webp&q=75)

## The pied-à-terre: Stamba Hotel

_14 Merab Kostava St._

Where would Tbilisi be without [Stamba Hotel](https://stambahotel.com/) and its Adjara Group brethren ([Fabrika](https://fabrikatbilisi.com/) and [Rooms](https://roomshotels.com/hotel/tbilisi/))? It certainly wouldn’t be topping lists of the trendiest cities on earth. Stamba is one of my favorite hotels anywhere, in part because it’s aesthetically unplaceable: Look one way and you’ll see thickets of cacti; look another and there are supple, snaking leather sofas; look up and ceiling-mounted machinery that once shuttled papers along a conveyor belt still looms overhead, a reminder of the building’s origins as a Soviet printing house. If you stay here, book an Aviator room, outfitted with a freestanding brass tub, a La Marzocco espresso machine, and a McIntosh stereo system.

But what puts Stamba in an echelon all its own is its self-contained cultural ecosystem that locals enjoy as much as guests. You could happily spend a whole day here, and I occasionally do, swanning from the café with its house-roasted beans to the Japanese-ish teriyaki joint to Warehouse, my beloved nook for deep-cut natural wines. Somewhere in there, I’ll inevitably wind up at the white-tablecloth restaurant for an Adjaruli khachapuri, that molten cheesy canoe topped with egg yolk and butter that you gloop together with a spoon. Come sundown, everyone spills into the enormous courtyard out back, which swells into a wine-sloshed scene.

![Image 8: The pied-à-terre: Stamba Hotel](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/5hjdg48wuSu0yjKQoiDAdt/fb75a0b571f76e14dd2a6154842f5844/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Stamba_Hotel.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## Holy-grail Imeruli khachapuri: Shavi Lomi

_30 Zurab Kvlividze St._

[Shavi Lomi](https://www.instagram.com/shavilomi_tbilisicuisine/?hl=es) occupies a creaky old house filled with patterned tablecloths, cats flitting between tables, and the buttery glow of antique light fixtures. In an era of “concept” restaurants, Shavi Lomi is refreshingly analog: It’s about providing comfort, nourishment, and maybe even a sense of homecoming.

Chef Meriko Gubeladze, the owner and my cookbook coauthor, is something of a household name in Georgia: She hosted a primetime cooking show for a decade and cooked for Anthony Bourdain when _Parts Unknown_ came to Tbilisi. Originally from Imereti, she makes the finest version I’ve tried of her region’s namesake khachapuri: a dinner plate-size, double-crusted pie filled with tangy, curdy cheese. It’s soft, foldy, and not too doughy—perfect alongside Gurian black tea at breakfast or dipped into tkemali (sour plum sauce) for a snack.

![Image 9: Holy-grail Imeruli khachapuri: Shavi Lomi](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/5x88OZSpXUqgEqRhgypFGF/dcc2121a136228a93255fc38fb1ce871/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Shavi_Lomi.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## Surprising Soviet crafts: Navtlughi Market

_Mevele Dead End_

Dry Bridge flea market is Tbilisi’s legendary antiquing stop, but in recent years, the quality has slipped, and there’s a nagging sense that you’re often picking through the dregs. Not so at Navtlughi, a ramshackle maze of sheds and market stalls on the fringes of town where you can shop for traditional hand-whittled mtsvadi (kebab) skewers, Caucasian rugs woven deep in the mountains on long-retired looms, beeswax candles made by monks, and enough bric-à-brac to make a packrat short-circuit. On a recent visit, I was hellbent on finding a Soviet gluggle and matching shot-glass set. Manufactured mostly in Ukraine and gilded by hand, these fish pitchers with gaping maws are hilarious to look at—and increasingly scarce. With one of these on the table, there’s no better way to wrangle your friends into a round of chacha, Georgia’s fiery grape brandy.

![Image 10: Surprising Soviet crafts: Navtlughi Market](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/3yfI8PP0pFbQW8Hg32pMZ1/6cc940f9657c382f059c2063ed4388bc/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Navtlughi_Market.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The fashion fix: Archived Couture

_12 Leo Kiacheli St._

Eight years ago, Luka Gviniashvili started amassing what has become perhaps the world’s largest private collection of Christian Lacroix, and today it’s on display at his three-year-old boutique, [Archive Couture](https://archivedcouture.com/). The space was conceived with Lacroix himself and channels his gloriously OTT ’80s salons with lipstick-red floors and black ornamental flourishes. The collection is just as exuberant, mixing Lacroix haute couture and ready-to-wear with 20th-century fashion, jewelry, historical textiles, and even liturgical vestments. It’s technically an archive, but don’t expect white gloves and hushed voices: You can wander in off the street, get up close to the clothes, and, crucially, buy whatever you see.

![Image 11: The fashion fix: Archived Couture](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/2Bs70WC5czEGoa7A9mIwsj/c221eb833ef9083248df08cd2312bd96/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Archived_Couture.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The edible haul: Dezerter’s Bazaar

_5 Abastumani St._

One of Georgia's most eye-catching foods is churchkhela, a knobbly confection made by dipping strings of nuts (usually walnuts, sometimes hazelnuts) repeatedly into thickened, sweetened grape juice. It’s something of a primordial power bar: Georgian soldiers are said to have loaded their saddlebags with them before heading into battle. Today you can buy churchkhela just about everywhere for your own road trips and cheese boards, but the best are handmade and sold at markets like Dezerter's Bazaar. Look for pale brownish-pink ones that still bend slightly in the middle, and avoid anything stiff, cracked, or artificially colored. While you’re at the bazaar, stock up on Georgia’s holy trinity of spices: coriander, dried marigold, and blue fenugreek. To find my spice angel, Shazina, amid the throngs, simply ask a friendly (ideally non-spice) vendor to point you in the direction of Shazina, “the spice lady.”

![Image 12: The edible haul: Dezerter’s Bazaar](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/6Bb1UxFTkQXiua3tBui0f5/3c61a17e7da89799c036d68af0dfeaed/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Spices_from_Dezerters_Bazaar.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The unsung cultural stop: Silk Museum

_6 Giorgi Tsabadze St._

Tbilisi’s [State Silk Museum](https://silkmuseum.ge/) celebrates the strange alchemy of turning silkworm spit into finery. Silk was once serious business in Georgia: Mulberry trees grew across the country to feed armies of ravenous silkworms, whose cocoons supplied a thriving local industry. Founded in the late 19th century as part of the Caucasian Sericulture Station, the museum gets wonderfully granular about the whole process, with cocoons, antique looms, shimmering textiles, and other silky arcana. After a respectful four-year restoration, it reopened in 2024 to little fanfare, still decked out with its original display cases, patterned floors, and intricately carved woodwork. Even if you’re not obsessed with silk, the redbrick building alone is worth the detour.

![Image 13: The unsung cultural stop: Silk Museum](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/2pGSFpWxY9P2G6sjw19CPz/5c2651c6459d55e60c711ee47090db89/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Silk_Museum.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## My architectural crush: Bank of Georgia Headquarters

_29a Iuri Gagarini St._

The Bank of Georgia headquarters is a hulking Jenga tower of concrete slabs cantilevered over a wooded slope above the Mtkvari. To this day, every time I drive past it on the highway, I crane my neck out the window to get a better look. Built in 1975 as the headquarters of the Georgian SSR’s Ministry of Highway Construction, it’s a Soviet Brutalist triumph that looks as though half of it is floating in midair.

But since it’s hard to visit in person, I’ll send you instead to the Persian Mirror Halls at the Tbilisi State Academy of Arts, where, inside a 19th-century mansion, you’ll find fairytale rooms encrusted with Qajar-style mirrorwork. Installed by Persian craftsmen, the tiny shards of glass tessellate the walls and ceilings alongside painted flowers and nature motifs; stained-glass windows throw colored light across the whole confection. It’s a wondrous bit of Tehran hiding in central Tbilisi.

![Image 14: My architectural crush: Bank of Georgia Headquarters](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/6m4PT1CGNNxjoGxdrvaClg/4ae8ff2477ace6962d56191cf9dad6da/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Bank_of_Georgia_Headquarters.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The daytime hangout: Honoré

_4 Constitution St._

[Honoré](https://www.instagram.com/honore.tbilisi/?hl=es) occupies an old building whose renovation left its bones on full display: Soaring gallery windows and battered columns contrast with a wraparound cocktail bar, a killer sound system, and a garden with picnic tables where you can watch mtsvadi sputter over the coals. I like it best during the day, when things are quiet enough to post up by the windows and watch cats wander in from the garden and toast themselves on the radiators. I’ll often sit for hours, starting with lunch—always the (unfortunately named) “bean plate,” a heap of spicy beans with sharp Guda cheese and a whole cucumber thwacked open and salted—then move on to coffee, maybe dessert, then another coffee, working or reading all the while.

![Image 15: The daytime hangout: Honoré](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/7pITkDZQXL66m9APWSg05V/3dbaabb60910f2b028eaf8905576d69d/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Honore.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The scavenger hunt: Tbilisi Gold Market

_Tbilisi Central Station_

The Tbilisi Gold Market packs some of the city’s most precious specimens into an unlikely setting: the ground floor of a gritty train station, a late-Soviet concrete pile with a space-age sweep to its facade. Inside, the sheer volume of tchotchkes can scramble your brain, so go with at least a vague idea of what you’re hunting for, whether it’s a gold bracelet, a Soviet watch, or an antique niello-silver cigarette case. It’s worth haggling until the cows come home, and if you’re buying actual gold, have the piece tested before you pay: There’s a lab at the back of the market that offers a free service.

![Image 16: The scavenger hunt: Tbilisi Gold Market](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/5rjeJzLvCKnNigyYiN8OEB/1e96680ce7c2a4df06395d24381d3e02/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Gold_Market.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The dinner spot: Ninia’s Garden

_97 Dimitri Uznadze St._

If Shavi Lomi is Gubeladze in grandmotherly mode—all snug rooms and lovingly prepared Georgian staples—[Ninia’s Garden](https://www.instagram.com/ninias_garden/?hl=en) is where she lets her creativity fully unspool. A tomato salad comes with hunks of sourdough made from doli, a salvaged ancient Georgian red wheat; ajapsandali, the normally ratatouille-like combination of eggplant, peppers, and tomato, goes from amorphous to geometrical with crisp batons of fried eggplant; and a waffle arrives under yogurt cream and glossy beet confit. The cooking is playful, but never so cheffy that you lose sight of what you’re eating.

![Image 17: The dinner spot: Ninia’s Garden](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/YlvwldBwpAfWUKO6BFhwF/93c13effbf156b244fb97a6fd110741e/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Ninias_Garden.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The side quest: Chronicle of Georgia

_Chronicle of Georgia_

Started in 1985 by Georgian sculptor Zurab Tsereteli, the Chronicle of Georgia was built to memorialize the nation’s history, with 16 colossal pillars depicting Georgian royalty and epic battles interspersed with scenes from the life of Christ. It was never completed, which explains the blank panels and bare concrete. Wandering between its 100-foot-tall bronze figures is like stumbling into some ancient fantastical kingdom where a pterodactyl could swoop down at any moment.

![Image 18: The side quest: Chronicle of Georgia](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/7x2VCpEUj69zCsG5H2JKb6/da3c28fa5337dbbd9e8c174b927a952a/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Chronicle_of_Georgia.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The culinary deep cut: Pingvinebi

_Zhiuli Shartava Street_

I only found Pingvinebi because a friend tipped me off, and even after decades in business, most Tbilisians have no idea it exists. The no-frills room has tiled floors, a jukebox jerry-rigged to staticky speakers, tables of men clacking backgammon pieces and swigging Kazbegi beer, and prices that remind me of when I first came to Georgia, when almost nothing cost more than a few bucks.

God only knows why it’s called “Penguins,” a theme carried through with stuffed penguins and paintings on the walls. Order the spicy, tomatoey “soup” kharcho and katleti (pan-fried beef patties) with mashed potatoes, then peek into the kitchen, where women in splotched aprons stir enormous pots of stews in varying shades of orange, red, and brown. Nobody speaks much English, so this is where Google Translate comes in handy; it’s cash only, too.

![Image 19: The culinary deep cut: Pingvinebi](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/4brZibBtHKbNZM4CjpDGsO/d2ad15512d05357899029ccc8625bf20/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Pingvinebi.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## Walk-ins-welcome poliphony: Sioni Cathedral

_3 Sioni St._

One of the easiest ways to hear Georgia’s UNESCO-protected polyphony requires neither a ticket nor a reservation: just walk into Sioni Basilica during Sunday liturgy. Beneath the cathedral’s stone vaults, groups of men chant a cappella, their voices splitting into separate lines before intertwining again in harmonies that seem to set the walls vibrating. Services generally get going around 10 a.m., with worshippers drifting in and out throughout, so you can quietly do the same. It's best to stand toward the back and to dress conservatively.

![Image 20: Walk-ins-welcome poliphony: Sioni Cathedral](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/1QeCd8VfTj67fivioeiyeb/3b186f964416b675eebba063d9f31150/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Sioni_Basilica.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The edible time warp: Mapshalia

_137 Davit Aghmashenebeli Ave._

Mapshalia is one of Tbilisi’s old guard, opened by Elsa Kalandia in 1980 and serving the food of her native Samegrelo. Its dining room has a huge Soviet-era bas-relief carved into the walls, laminated menus with home-snapped photos of the food, and buckets of clay-oven bread propped behind the register. The crowd is a mix of old-timers reading newspapers and backpackers who’ve gotten wind of the prices. Not only is Mapshalia’s lobio (spicy bean stew) the best in the city—with fearless chili kick and generous fistfuls of cilantro—it’s probably the cheapest, too, at about two bucks a bowl.

![Image 21: The edible time warp: Mapshalia](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/3M6ZGgYUV6JpUlGusBmrWT/14150769a15a1c966fc66b0ed7adfb5e/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Mapshalia.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## Dumpling heaven: Pictograma

_31 Atoneli St._

[Pictograma](https://www.instagram.com/pict_ograma/?hl=en) is Tbilisi’s only restaurant devoted to the food of Khevsureti, the highland region known for its warrens of stone tower villages and hearty shepherd’s cooking. Most khinkali you’ll encounter in the capital are kalakuri, or “city-style,” stuffed with a cilantro-flecked mixture of pork and beef. Here they make the mtiuluri variety still eaten by Khevsur shepherds today: beef only, onion, and plenty of caraway, all bundled inside dough that’s rolled and pleated by hand. You can feel the difference—the wrapper isn’t factory-smooth but pleasantly textured and a little irregular. Just beware the gush of broth on your first bite, lest you spend the rest of lunch wearing it.

![Image 22: Dumpling heaven: Pictograma](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/3FobgFmtZ8WMtmTXdioZBF/c2af487323618e704433f10b9b517ffa/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Piktograma.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## An address off the radar: The Blue House (Gabashvili House)

_54 Shota Rustaveli Avenue_

You could walk down Rustaveli Avenue a hundred times and never clock the Blue House, but duck through an unassuming passageway at number 54 and suddenly, there it is: the 1897 Gabashvili House, all turquoise balconies, carved balusters, intricate fretwork, and staircases zigzagging Escher-style around a quiet courtyard. It later became home to physician Nikoloz Kipshidze—whose patient list reportedly included Stalin—but the real thrill is simply finding it. People still live here, so poke around respectfully, then slip back out onto Rustaveli feeling slightly smug that you know it exists.

![Image 23: An address off the radar: The Blue House (Gabashvili House)](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/6Ba6J9TMHVvBqkUJ25AqlX/fb0963d55385aefa134c284aab1f4c9e/10.3.26_Tbilisi_The_Blue_House.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## A nightcap, naturally: 41° Art of Drinks

_19 Galaktion Tabidze St._

Heave open the heavy sliding door, pad down a spiral staircase, and you’re in this [rakish cocktail lair](https://www.instagram.com/41gradus/?hl=es) where Georgian ingredients get shaken, stirred, and spiked. One drink made with pine liqueur tastes like licking a Christmas tree (in a good way) and conjures nostalgic holiday memories; another foamy number, with lemon and matsoni (Georgian yogurt), is tangy, sour, and a little salty.

## The pied-à-terre: Stamba Hotel

_14 Merab Kostava St._

Where would Tbilisi be without [Stamba Hotel](https://stambahotel.com/) and its Adjara Group brethren ([Fabrika](https://fabrikatbilisi.com/) and [Rooms](https://roomshotels.com/hotel/tbilisi/))? It certainly wouldn’t be topping lists of the trendiest cities on earth. Stamba is one of my favorite hotels anywhere, in part because it’s aesthetically unplaceable: Look one way and you’ll see thickets of cacti; look another and there are supple, snaking leather sofas; look up and ceiling-mounted machinery that once shuttled papers along a conveyor belt still looms overhead, a reminder of the building’s origins as a Soviet printing house. If you stay here, book an Aviator room, outfitted with a freestanding brass tub, a La Marzocco espresso machine, and a McIntosh stereo system.

But what puts Stamba in an echelon all its own is its self-contained cultural ecosystem that locals enjoy as much as guests. You could happily spend a whole day here, and I occasionally do, swanning from the café with its house-roasted beans to the Japanese-ish teriyaki joint to Warehouse, my beloved nook for deep-cut natural wines. Somewhere in there, I’ll inevitably wind up at the white-tablecloth restaurant for an Adjaruli khachapuri, that molten cheesy canoe topped with egg yolk and butter that you gloop together with a spoon. Come sundown, everyone spills into the enormous courtyard out back, which swells into a wine-sloshed scene.

## Holy-grail Imeruli khachapuri: Shavi Lomi

_30 Zurab Kvlividze St._

[Shavi Lomi](https://www.instagram.com/shavilomi_tbilisicuisine/?hl=es) occupies a creaky old house filled with patterned tablecloths, cats flitting between tables, and the buttery glow of antique light fixtures. In an era of “concept” restaurants, Shavi Lomi is refreshingly analog: It’s about providing comfort, nourishment, and maybe even a sense of homecoming.

Chef Meriko Gubeladze, the owner and my cookbook coauthor, is something of a household name in Georgia: She hosted a primetime cooking show for a decade and cooked for Anthony Bourdain when _Parts Unknown_ came to Tbilisi. Originally from Imereti, she makes the finest version I’ve tried of her region’s namesake khachapuri: a dinner plate-size, double-crusted pie filled with tangy, curdy cheese. It’s soft, foldy, and not too doughy—perfect alongside Gurian black tea at breakfast or dipped into tkemali (sour plum sauce) for a snack.

![Image 28: Holy-grail Imeruli khachapuri: Shavi Lomi](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/5x88OZSpXUqgEqRhgypFGF/dcc2121a136228a93255fc38fb1ce871/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Shavi_Lomi.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## Surprising Soviet crafts: Navtlughi Market

_Mevele Dead End_

Dry Bridge flea market is Tbilisi’s legendary antiquing stop, but in recent years, the quality has slipped, and there’s a nagging sense that you’re often picking through the dregs. Not so at Navtlughi, a ramshackle maze of sheds and market stalls on the fringes of town where you can shop for traditional hand-whittled mtsvadi (kebab) skewers, Caucasian rugs woven deep in the mountains on long-retired looms, beeswax candles made by monks, and enough bric-à-brac to make a packrat short-circuit. On a recent visit, I was hellbent on finding a Soviet gluggle and matching shot-glass set. Manufactured mostly in Ukraine and gilded by hand, these fish pitchers with gaping maws are hilarious to look at—and increasingly scarce. With one of these on the table, there’s no better way to wrangle your friends into a round of chacha, Georgia’s fiery grape brandy.

![Image 29: Surprising Soviet crafts: Navtlughi Market](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/3yfI8PP0pFbQW8Hg32pMZ1/6cc940f9657c382f059c2063ed4388bc/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Navtlughi_Market.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The fashion fix: Archived Couture

_12 Leo Kiacheli St._

Eight years ago, Luka Gviniashvili started amassing what has become perhaps the world’s largest private collection of Christian Lacroix, and today it’s on display at his three-year-old boutique, [Archive Couture](https://archivedcouture.com/). The space was conceived with Lacroix himself and channels his gloriously OTT ’80s salons with lipstick-red floors and black ornamental flourishes. The collection is just as exuberant, mixing Lacroix haute couture and ready-to-wear with 20th-century fashion, jewelry, historical textiles, and even liturgical vestments. It’s technically an archive, but don’t expect white gloves and hushed voices: You can wander in off the street, get up close to the clothes, and, crucially, buy whatever you see.

## The edible haul: Dezerter’s Bazaar

_5 Abastumani St._

One of Georgia's most eye-catching foods is churchkhela, a knobbly confection made by dipping strings of nuts (usually walnuts, sometimes hazelnuts) repeatedly into thickened, sweetened grape juice. It’s something of a primordial power bar: Georgian soldiers are said to have loaded their saddlebags with them before heading into battle. Today you can buy churchkhela just about everywhere for your own road trips and cheese boards, but the best are handmade and sold at markets like Dezerter's Bazaar. Look for pale brownish-pink ones that still bend slightly in the middle, and avoid anything stiff, cracked, or artificially colored. While you’re at the bazaar, stock up on Georgia’s holy trinity of spices: coriander, dried marigold, and blue fenugreek. To find my spice angel, Shazina, amid the throngs, simply ask a friendly (ideally non-spice) vendor to point you in the direction of Shazina, “the spice lady.”

![Image 31: The edible haul: Dezerter’s Bazaar](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/6Bb1UxFTkQXiua3tBui0f5/3c61a17e7da89799c036d68af0dfeaed/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Spices_from_Dezerters_Bazaar.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The unsung cultural stop: Silk Museum

_6 Giorgi Tsabadze St._

Tbilisi’s [State Silk Museum](https://silkmuseum.ge/) celebrates the strange alchemy of turning silkworm spit into finery. Silk was once serious business in Georgia: Mulberry trees grew across the country to feed armies of ravenous silkworms, whose cocoons supplied a thriving local industry. Founded in the late 19th century as part of the Caucasian Sericulture Station, the museum gets wonderfully granular about the whole process, with cocoons, antique looms, shimmering textiles, and other silky arcana. After a respectful four-year restoration, it reopened in 2024 to little fanfare, still decked out with its original display cases, patterned floors, and intricately carved woodwork. Even if you’re not obsessed with silk, the redbrick building alone is worth the detour.

![Image 32: The unsung cultural stop: Silk Museum](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/2pGSFpWxY9P2G6sjw19CPz/5c2651c6459d55e60c711ee47090db89/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Silk_Museum.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## My architectural crush: Bank of Georgia Headquarters

_29a Iuri Gagarini St._

The Bank of Georgia headquarters is a hulking Jenga tower of concrete slabs cantilevered over a wooded slope above the Mtkvari. To this day, every time I drive past it on the highway, I crane my neck out the window to get a better look. Built in 1975 as the headquarters of the Georgian SSR’s Ministry of Highway Construction, it’s a Soviet Brutalist triumph that looks as though half of it is floating in midair.

But since it’s hard to visit in person, I’ll send you instead to the Persian Mirror Halls at the Tbilisi State Academy of Arts, where, inside a 19th-century mansion, you’ll find fairytale rooms encrusted with Qajar-style mirrorwork. Installed by Persian craftsmen, the tiny shards of glass tessellate the walls and ceilings alongside painted flowers and nature motifs; stained-glass windows throw colored light across the whole confection. It’s a wondrous bit of Tehran hiding in central Tbilisi.

![Image 33: My architectural crush: Bank of Georgia Headquarters](https://images.ctfassets.net/6alb7q886wpg/6m4PT1CGNNxjoGxdrvaClg/4ae8ff2477ace6962d56191cf9dad6da/10.3.26_Tbilisi_Bank_of_Georgia_Headquarters.png?w=1920&fm=webp&q=75)

## The daytime hangout: Honoré

_4 Constitution St._

[Honoré](https://www.instagram.com/honore.tbilisi/?hl=es) occupies an old building whose renovation left its bones on full display: Soaring gallery windows and battered columns contrast with a wraparound cocktail bar, a killer sound system, and a garden with picnic tables where you can watch mtsvadi sputter over the coals. I like it best during the day, when things are quiet enough to post up by the windows and watch cats wander in from the garden and toast themselves on the radiators. I’ll often sit for hours, starting with lunch—always the (unfortunately named) “bean plate,” a heap of spicy beans with sharp Guda cheese and a whole cucumber thwacked open and salted—then move on to coffee, maybe dessert, then another coffee, working or reading all the while.

## The scavenger hunt: Tbilisi Gold Market

_Tbilisi Central Station_

The Tbilisi Gold Market packs some of the city’s most precious specimens into an unlikely setting: the ground floor of a gritty train station, a late-Soviet concrete pile with a space-age sweep to its facade. Inside, the sheer volume of tchotchkes can scramble your brain, so go with at least a vague idea of what you’re hunting for, whether it’s a gold bracelet, a Soviet watch, or an antique niello-silver cigarette case. It’s worth haggling until the cows come home, and if you’re buying actual gold, have the piece tested before you pay: There’s a lab at the back of the market that offers a free service.

## The dinner spot: Ninia’s Garden

_97 Dimitri Uznadze St._

If Shavi Lomi is Gubeladze in grandmotherly mode—all snug rooms and lovingly prepared Georgian staples—[Ninia’s Garden](https://www.instagram.com/ninias_garden/?hl=en) is where she lets her creativity fully unspool. A tomato salad comes with hunks of sourdough made from doli, a salvaged ancient Georgian red wheat; ajapsandali, the normally ratatouille-like combination of eggplant, peppers, and tomato, goes from amorphous to geometrical with crisp batons of fried eggplant; and a waffle arrives under yogurt cream and glossy beet confit. ## The side quest: Chronicle of Georgia

_Chronicle of Georgia_

Started in 1985 by Georgian sculptor Zurab Tsereteli, the Chronicle of Georgia was built to memorialize the nation’s history, with 16 colossal pillars depicting Georgian royalty and epic battles interspersed with scenes from the life of Christ. It was never completed, which explains the blank panels and bare concrete. Wandering between its 100-foot-tall bronze figures is like stumbling into some ancient fantastical kingdom where a pterodactyl could swoop down at any moment.

## The culinary deep cut: Pingvinebi

_Zhiuli Shartava Street_

I only found Pingvinebi because a friend tipped me off, and even after decades in business, most Tbilisians have no idea it exists. The no-frills room has tiled floors, a jukebox jerry-rigged to staticky speakers, tables of men clacking backgammon pieces and swigging Kazbegi beer, and prices that remind me of when I first came to Georgia, when almost nothing cost more than a few bucks.

God only knows why it’s called “Penguins,” a theme carried through with stuffed penguins and paintings on the walls. Order the spicy, tomatoey “soup” kharcho and katleti (pan-fried beef patties) with mashed potatoes, then peek into the kitchen, where women in splotched aprons stir enormous pots of stews in varying shades of orange, red, and brown. ## Walk-ins-welcome poliphony: Sioni Cathedral

_3 Sioni St._

One of the easiest ways to hear Georgia’s UNESCO-protected polyphony requires neither a ticket nor a reservation: just walk into Sioni Basilica during Sunday liturgy. Beneath the cathedral’s stone vaults, groups of men chant a cappella, their voices splitting into separate lines before intertwining again in harmonies that seem to set the walls vibrating. Services generally get going around 10 a.m., with worshippers drifting in and out throughout, so you can quietly do the same. It's best to stand toward the back and to dress conservatively.

## The edible time warp: Mapshalia

_137 Davit Aghmashenebeli Ave._

Mapshalia is one of Tbilisi’s old guard, opened by Elsa Kalandia in 1980 and serving the food of her native Samegrelo. The crowd is a mix of old-timers reading newspapers and backpackers who’ve gotten wind of the prices. Not only is Mapshalia’s lobio (spicy bean stew) the best in the city—with fearless chili kick and generous fistfuls of cilantro—it’s probably the cheapest, too, at about two bucks a bowl.

## Dumpling heaven: Pictograma

_31 Atoneli St._

[Pictograma](https://www.instagram.com/pict_ograma/?hl=en) is Tbilisi’s only restaurant devoted to the food of Khevsureti, the highland region known for its warrens of stone tower villages and hearty shepherd’s cooking. Most khinkali you’ll encounter in the capital are kalakuri, or “city-style,” stuffed with a cilantro-flecked mixture of pork and beef. You can feel the difference—the wrapper isn’t factory-smooth but pleasantly textured and a little irregular. Just beware the gush of broth on your first bite, lest you spend the rest of lunch wearing it.

# Regal Cinema

## The modern cinema that set the ball rolling for Mumbai’s Art Deco.

[](link_0)[](link_0)

[By Art Deco Mumbai](link_33)

Regal Cinema was inaugurated on 14 October, 1933, with the Laurel and Hardy comedy,_The Devil’s Brother_. As Bombay’s first Art Deco cinema, it was a breakaway from the Victorian Gothic and Indo-Saracenic structures in its vicinity.

Cinema prgramme for Regal Cinema, Dated 10 July 1937 (1937)**Art Deco Mumbai**

It was commissioned by Framji Sidhwa and his friend KA Kooka, who ran the Calcutta-based Globe Theatres.

Perspective view of Regal Cinema (2017/2017)**Art Deco Mumbai**

Charles Frederick Stevens designed the cinema. Interestingly, his father Frederick William Stevens, designed the Victoria Terminus (now known as Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus), a towering 19th century railway station in the Victorian Gothic style.

Aerial view of Wellington Circle, Mumbai**Original Source: Jehangir Sorabjee Archive**

In its architecture, the cinema was sensitively designed to echo the spirit of the skyline of gables, turrets and domes, which characterise the Wellington Fountain circle on which the Regal was built.

The cinema was truly ahead of its time. It was fully air-conditioned, had an underground parking, an elevator, and even a special telephone attached to the seats for the hearing impaired to follow what was said on screen.

With concealed lights and central air-conditioning, the ceiling had a "clean appearance", free from suspended lights and fans obstructing the design.

Cinema programme for Regal Cinema, Dated December 1938 (1938)**Art Deco Mumbai**

Karl Schara, the Czechoslovakian artist, designed the interiors with bold sunray cubist motifs in pale orange and jade green, in harmony with the modern simplicity of the exteriors. Many of the original embellishments, however, were obliterated during renovations in 1953.

On either side of the screen, intricately carved theatre masks representing Tragedy and Comedy are displayed on the walls - a reference to Shakespeare’s Globe Theatre.

Close-up view of the facade of Regal Cinema (2017/2017)**Art Deco Mumbai**

Similar murals can also be seen on the building’s facade, on either side of the theatre’s name. At one time, the lettering used to be lit up in neon.

Another interesting feature, on the steps leading up to the balcony, is the Oscar trophy etched into a mirror panel – an homage to the theatre's early association with Hollywood films.

Regal was comparable to the luxurious cinema houses in the West. Special attention was paid to comfort, with multiple entrances into the balcony and boxes, and seats imported from London. The magnificent theatre accommodated 1200 patrons at once.

A street-corner building, it boasted of a soda fountain with a side entrance on its ground floor. It became a hub for quick refreshments, whether for patrons or passersby.

Regal Cinema, Mumbai (2019/2019) by Shubhika Malara**Art Deco Mumbai**

An enduring landmark in Mumbai’s Colaba area, Regal Cinema marks the beginnings of a new epoch as the city entered a modern era.

# When going to the movies was an art- by Yoshita Sengupta, Mumbai Mirror

Jun 22, 2017

![Image 3](https://www.artdecomumbai.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/RN-CI-Going-to-movies-was-art-4a.jpg.webp)

It was a regular school day back in 1957 when a group of primary students of Rosary High School from Dockyard Road in Mazgaon made the trip to Colaba. It was to catch a screening of Alfred Hitchcock’s thriller Rope. The venue — Regal cinema.

One of the boys, then five, was hooked enough to spend the rest of his life making repeated trips. Rafique Bagdadi, now a noted film critic and one among Mumbai’s best-known amateur historians, is brimming with stories of the glorious days. “Going to Regal was like going to Rome or another European city. Behind it was the Taj Mahal hotel. In front of it stood the majestic Cowasji Jehangir Public Hall, which is now the NGMA. The insides of the theatre were as dreamy as the set of Hollywood films screened here,” he says of the Art Deco architecture style that Regal shares with other South Mumbai cinemas like Liberty and Eros. Inaugurated on October 14, 1933 by Mumbai governor Sir Frederick Sykus, Regal was built by film exhibitor Framji Sidhwa and his friend KA Kooka. And it had quite a few firsts to its credit. Asia’s first centrally air-conditioned theatre, it was also the first to introduce Cinemascope and offer basement car parking to its patrons. The reinforced concrete structure built at a lavish cost was conceived by Charles Stevens, son of famous 19th century English architect Fredrick Williams Stevens, while the interiors were designed by Czechoslovakian artist Karl Schara. Old-timers remember the sun ray Cubist motif in orange and jade green in the atrium.

For Deepak Rao, retired IPS officer and member of the Bombay Local History Society, Regal stands for an afternoon Arlem beer. While working at the Mumbai police headquarters across the road from the cinema, he’d hop over to its refreshment room that could house no more than six guests.

Regal’s historic value precedes its construction, says Rao. “The lane behind Regal is not named Battery Street for nothing. The site at Apollo Bunder on which the cinema stands was owned by the British army, and was occupied by an old saluting battery. When viceroys and VIPs arrived, they were greeted with a gun salute. The British government decided to lease the property in 1926, which is when it was acquired by Mr Sidhwa and Mr Kooka of Globe Theatre Ltd.,” says the 62-year-old.

Sidhwa’s life, say documents, was as dramatic as the movies he screened. Born in 1883 in Tarapore, Gujarat, in a middle-class home, he moved to an orphanage in Parel before gaining admission to Bharda New High School, which stands right beside the theatre he would build in 1928 — Capitol at VT. The student of St Xavier’s College had to drop out due to thinning finances and move to Rangoon in 1903 to find a job. Starting out as a clerk in Singer, he later took up an insurance job.

It was in 1913 that he established a small syndicate and launched his film exhibition business in Rangoon. Two years later, Globe Theatre Ltd. was born.

“Behram Contractor, in one of his essays, said going to the cinema was an art,” says Rao. And Regal played its part.

Baghdadi calls it an “experience” — South Bombay movie lovers would book tickets way in advance, dress up in finery and land up at the movies. “There was a soda fountain, a pantry for balcony audiences, and we’d dig into ice cream while musicians would perform live,” he shares.

Social worker, champion bridge player and MP Milind Deora’s mother Hema Deora’s memories of Regal stand testimony to Baghdadi’s description. As a 10-year-old in the early 1960s, Deora didn’t understand cinema, but that hardly mattered. “For me, the draw was the ice cream served in the cinema’s restaurant. The cup resembled a wine glass. It was a family affair. I’d wear my best dress, and we’d return home in a Tonga,” Deora reminisces.

Art deco movie theatre in Mumbai, India

Not to be confused with [Regal Cinemas](link_3).

For other uses, see [Regal Cinema (disambiguation)](link_4).

Regal Cinema, c. 1935

The **Regal Cinema** is an [art deco](link_19)[movie theatre](link_20) located at [Colaba Causeway](link_21), in [Mumbai](link_8), [India](link_9).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regal_Cinema#cite_note-tom2008-1) Built by Framji Sidhwa, the first film to be aired at the Regal was the [Laurel and Hardy](link_22) work _[The Devil's Brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Devil [link_23]'s\_Brother "The Devil's Brother")_ in 1933.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regal_Cinema#cite_note-toi2009-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regal_Cinema#cite_note-Rangan-3)

According to the _[Limca Book of Records](link_24)_, it is the first air conditioned theatre of India.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regal_Cinema#cite_note-4)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Regal_Cinema&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Regal Cinema was built during the cinema boom of the 1930s during which Plaza Central, New Empire, Broadway, Eros and [Metro](link_25) all opened in Mumbai. Opened in 1933, Regal was designed by [Charles Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Stevens_(architect)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Charles Stevens (architect) (page does not exist)"), the son of the famous 19th century architect [F. W. Stevens](link_26). Its interiors with extensive mirror-work were designed by the Czech artist [Karl Schara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Schara?action=edit&redlink=1 "Karl Schara (page does not exist)"). The main auditorium had a motif of sunrays in pale orange and jade green. Its interiors were designed to create an impression of airiness, coolness and size in harmony with the modern simplicity of the exteriors. The Regal was built completely in reinforced concrete cement (RCC), fully air conditioned, and had an underground parking lot for patrons. The elevator up from the parking area was a major innovation at the time.

The cinema was the third venue to host the [Filmfare Awards](link_27) night.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regal_Cinema#cite_note-toi2005-5) Today, it is a multi-use building combining a cinema with shops at street level.

The Regal Cinema was the lead theatre hosting the 17th Mumbai Academy of Moving Image (MAMI), held in 2015, starting from Friday, 29 October 2015. Also, The Regal Cinema was the lead theatre hosting the 18th. Mumbai Academy of Moving Image (MAMI), held in 2016.

# Liberty Cinema, Mumbai

## Showplace of the nation

[](link_0)[](link_0)

[By Art Deco Mumbai](https://artsandculture.google.com/partner/art-deco-mumbai)

![Image 16](blob:https://artsandculture.google.com/f5899c79-5bce-408b-aca9-ff8c0bc7ebcd [link_22])

![Image 17](blob:https://artsandculture.google.com/f5899c79-5bce-408b-aca9-ff8c0bc7ebcd [link_22])

+

–

![Image 18](blob:https://artsandculture.google.com/f5899c79-5bce-408b-aca9-ff8c0bc7ebcd [link_22])

![Image 19](link_0)![Image 20](link_0)![Image 21](blob:https://artsandculture.google.com/0fef9f3e-ccd6-4917-b2de-f495fac42245 [link_23])![Image 22](link_0)![Image 23](link_0)![Image 24](blob:https://artsandculture.google.com/0a087a21-f162-4def-abe1-a6429caf1ed4 [link_24])![Image 25](blob:https://artsandculture.google.com/4bac4c1e-166a-4b6c-a869-6b9748a5889f [link_25])![Image 26](link_0)![Image 27](link_0)![Image 28](link_0)![Image 29](blob:https://artsandculture.google.com/48e6b2d6-201e-4b96-bca1-e32b7432648c [link_26])![Image 30](link_0)![Image 31](link_0)![Image 32](link_0)![Image 33](link_0)

Watercolour illustration of Liberty Cinema (2018-04/2018-04)**Art Deco Mumbai**

This magnificent Art Deco cinema sits within the Marine Lines neighbourhood, next to West End, South Mumbai’s Art Deco hotel.

![Image 34](blob:https://artsandculture.google.com/814728f7-c4bf-4b05-bc91-d75515163c6c [link_27])

![Image 35](blob:https://artsandculture.google.com/814728f7-c4bf-4b05-bc91-d75515163c6c [link_27])

+

–

![Image 36](blob:https://artsandculture.google.com/814728f7-c4bf-4b05-bc91-d75515163c6c [link_27])

![Image 37](link_0)![Image 38](link_0)![Image 39](link_0)![Image 40](blob:https://artsandculture.google.com/2d1dd4d9-b32e-4b11-b925-a72fb8bda9fb [link_28])![Image 41](blob:https://artsandculture.google.com/94254126-27da-45c1-b026-6ee2ab45a5e1 [link_29])![Image 42](link_0)![Image 43](link_0)![Image 44](blob:https://artsandculture.google.com/01633116-07a8-4d66-9148-ec60ba7be1b9 [link_30])![Image 45](link_0)

Front view of Liberty Cinema (1949-03/1949-03)**Art Deco Mumbai**

With its foundation laid in 1947, Liberty Cinema was named to celebrate India’s independence on 15th August 1947. It was built as a single screen theatre that showcased only Hindi cinema, popularly known as "Bollywood" today.

Ground breaking ceremony of Liberty Cinema Group Photograph taken at the ground breaking ceremony of Liberty Cinema (1947/1947)**Art Deco Mumbai**

Hoosein Family, land owner Manu Subedar & project architect Riddley Abbott with his wife were in attendance at the ground breaking ceremony of Liberty Cinema in 1947.

Ground breaking ceremony of Liberty Cinema Habib Hoosein (1947/1947)**Art Deco Mumbai**

Habib Hoosein built Liberty.  
  
To meet the need for entertainment of troops of the Allied Forces that were based in Bombay, Habib constructed 45 cinemas all over Bombay, including Liberty. This lead to the construction boom of cinema theatres.

Ground breaking ceremony of Liberty Cinema Manu Subedar (1947/1947)**Art Deco Mumbai**

Manu Subedar, eminent economist  
  
The land where Liberty Cinema was built was acquired from him.

Ground breaking ceremony of Liberty Cinema Mr and Mrs Riddley Abbott (1947/1947)**Art Deco Mumbai**

Mr and Mrs Riddley Abbott  
  
Riddley Abbott was the Architect of Liberty Cinema. After his untimely death in an air crash when he went on a vacation, it was J.B. Fernandes who was appointed the supervising architect. The stunning interiors were designed by W.M. Namjoshi

Ground breaking ceremony of Liberty Cinema Nazir Hoosein (1947/1947)**Art Deco Mumbai**

Nazir Hoosein, son of Habib Hoosein, owner of Liberty.  
  
By passion and profession a race car driver and F-1 aficionado

Poster of Andaaz**Art Deco Mumbai**

The theatre opened with the iconic Hindi film _Andaz_- starring superstars Raj Kapoor, Nargis and Dilip Kumar -on 21 March 1949.

Poster of Awaara (2018-06/2018-06)**Art Deco Mumbai**

Since 1949, every major Hindi blockbuster has been showcased at Liberty.

Poster of Mother India**Art Deco Mumbai**

_Awara_ and _Mother India_ were blockbusters that had a long run here.

[](link_31)

Eminent Actors of the Golden Era of Indian cinema (2018-06/2018-06)**Art Deco Mumbai**

Mini Theatre for private screening

Habib Hoosein hosted cinema personalities for social evenings (mehfil) in the Liberty ‘mini’ theatre - his private screening room. Raj Kapoor, a regular, would play the lilting tunes of _Awara_ on the theatre’s piano.

[Video 1](link_32)

Watch as the mini theatre comes alive with an incredible display of light and colour. The floral motifs on the ceiling are made with luminous paint, designed to glow during the light show.

Hum Aapke Hain Koun**Art Deco Mumbai**

In 1994 _Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!_ starring Madhuri Dixit and Salman Khan, opened at Liberty.

[Video 2](link_32)

At 125 weeks it was the longest running Hindi film at Liberty. It ran _house full_ for 44 consecutive weeks (3 times a day). Well over 2 million people saw it at Liberty.

[Video 3](link_33)

Mr. Hoosein recalls how legendary artist and painter M F Hussain saw the film over 60 times and danced barefoot in the aisles of the Stalls everytime Madhuri Dixit danced on the screen.

[](link_34)

The façades of Liberty Cinema in 2018 and 1952. (2018-07/2018-07)**Art Deco Mumbai**

Liberty Cinema as a Cultural Venue

The Liberty has always been a labour of love, with a lifetime of loyalty, care and affinity shown to it by its owners, long-standing staff and patrons. May its curtains never come down.

**Colaba Causeway**, officially known as **Shahid [Bhagat Singh](link_22) Road**, is a commercial street,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-1) and a major [causeway](link_23) or land link between [Colaba](link_0) and the [Old Woman's Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Woman [link_24]'s_Island "Old Woman's Island") in the city of [Mumbai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai "Mumbai"), [India](link_15).

It lies close to the [Fort](link_25) area, and to the east of [Cuffe Parade](link_26), an upmarket neighbourhood in [South Mumbai](link_27), and close by are Mumbai's famous landmarks, the [Gateway of India](link_28) and [Taj Mahal Palace & Tower](link_29).

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Colaba_Causeway&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [History of Mumbai](link_30)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Sevenislandsofbombay.png/120px-Sevenislandsofbombay.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sevenislandsofbombay.png)

Original seven islands of Bombay

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Colaba_Causeway_construction%2C_view_from_Colaba_island%2C_1826.jpg/250px-Colaba_Causeway_construction%2C_view_from_Colaba_island%2C_1826.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Colaba_Causeway_construction,_view_from_Colaba_island,_1826.jpg)

Colaba Causeway construction using timber, view from Colaba island, 1826

By the beginning of the nineteenth century, the Fort area and part of older town were overcrowded, as the island of Colaba, the southern tip of the city,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-2) had already been declared a [cantonment](link_31) area in 1796, barring all construction by the civilian population. Soon the boat traffic to area increased in the next few decades, and several people died due to the capsizing of overcrowded boats, making the construction of the causeway imperative.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-3) What also added to the urgency to its construction was that, [Mountstuart Elphinstone](link_32), [Governor of Bombay](link_33) (1819–1827), had already built the first home on [Malabar Hill](link_34), following which the rich quickly started moving into the centrally placed, Fort) area.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-4)

The Causeway as it is known to the locals, was constructed by the [British East India Company](link_35), during the tenure of [Sir Robert Grant](link_36) (1779–1838) as the governor of Bombay (1835–1838),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-5) and its construction completed in 1838, which used the Old Woman's Island as a part of it;[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-7) with this the last two islands of Colaba and Old Woman's Island (out of the [Seven islands of Bombay](link_37)), which were first taken in 1675, got connected with the mainland of [Bombay](link_38). Until 1839, Colaba was accessible only during the low tide, though soon it saw rapid development in the area, especially after the construction of the _Cotton Exchange_ at [Cotton Green](link_39) in 1844.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-8) The Causeway was later further widened in 1861 and 1863.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-hist-9)

Horse-drawn tram-cars were introduced here,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-10) in 1873 by Stearns and Kitteredge, for their offices on the west side of the Causeway, where the Electric House now stands.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-hist-9)

## Overview

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Colaba_Causeway&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Overview")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Metro_House_Colaba_Mumbai_Jul25_A7CR_05955.jpg/250px-Metro_House_Colaba_Mumbai_Jul25_A7CR_05955.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Metro_House_Colaba_Mumbai_Jul25_A7CR_05955.jpg)

Cafe Mondegar, Metro House, Colaba Causeway

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/LeopoldCafe_gobeirne.jpg/250px-LeopoldCafe_gobeirne.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LeopoldCafe_gobeirne.jpg)

Leopold Cafe and Bar, since 1871

Today, it is termed as the 'Culture Square' of Mumbai.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-blo-11) The architecture of the area is reminiscent of old Mumbai, fact highlighted by buildings like, [National Gallery of Modern Art](link_40) (NGMA), [Regal Cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regal_Cinema "Regal Cinema"), [Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Museum](link_41) and [Cusrow Baug](link_42), a [Parsi](link_43) residential colony built in 1934, covering an area of 84,000 square yards, which is home to over 500 families.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-12) Plus the area is also a hub of various art galleries, which makes this area a natural destination for artist community.

Apart from upmarket retail showrooms, and small shops dealing in electronic goods, cosmetics, clothes and music, it has a pavement book stall dating back several decades,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-13) besides having numerous small shops and footpath outlets selling everything from artifacts to shawls, carpets and minor antiques to slippers of all kinds, which makes tourists, backpackers and locals from South Mumbai throng the area all through the year.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colaba_Causeway#cite_note-blo-11)

# Art Deco Mumbai

## Mumbai, India

Mumbai hosts the second largest collection of Art Deco buildings in the world.

The Art Deco Mumbai Trust (ADM) is dedicated to raising awareness and appreciation, documenting this rich Deco heritage and advocating its conservation. Founded in 2016, its ongoing photo documentation has identified over 650 Art Deco buildings across the city. As part of its outreach, the Trust also hosts walking tours, public lectures and workshops.

The ADM website, the only one in the world, provides public access to a comprehensive repository of information on Mumbai’s Deco. ADM brings Art Deco heritage into Mumbai's mainstream dialogue on heritage and empowers stakeholders to make conscious decisions.

# Art Deco Mumbai

## Mumbai, India

Mumbai hosts the second largest collection of Art Deco buildings in the world.

The Art Deco Mumbai Trust (ADM) is dedicated to raising awareness and appreciation, documenting this rich Deco heritage and advocating its conservation. Founded in 2016, its ongoing photo documentation has identified over 650 Art Deco buildings across the city. As part of its outreach, the Trust also hosts walking tours, public lectures and workshops.

The ADM website, the only one in the world, provides public access to a comprehensive repository of information on Mumbai’s Deco. ADM brings Art Deco heritage into Mumbai's mainstream dialogue on heritage and empowers stakeholders to make conscious decisions.

# When going to the movies was an art

[Yoshita Sengupta](link_75) / Mumbai Mirror / Updated: Oct 28, 2012, 13:56 IST

Share

[](link_76)

AA

+**Text Size**
*   Small

[Follow us](link_77)

As Regal cinema enters its 80th year, here’s a look at the ‘theatre of firsts’

![Image 1: When going to the movies was an art](https://static.toiimg.com/thumb/msid-16990810,imgsize-20126,width-400,resizemode-4/16990810.jpg)

As Regal cinema enters its 80th year, here’s a look at the ‘theatre of firsts’  
 It was a regular school day back in 1957 when a group of primary students of Rosary High School from Dockyard Road in Mazgaon made the trip to Colaba. It was to catch a screening of [Alfred Hitchcock](link_78)’s thriller Rope. The venue — Regal cinema.   
 One of the boys, then five, was hooked enough to spend the rest of his life making repeated trips.

![Image 2: 1x1 polls](link_79)

Rafique Bagdadi, now a noted film critic and one among Mumbai’s bestknown amateur historians, is brimming with stories of the glorious days. “Going to Regal was like going to Rome or another European city. Behind it was the [Taj Mahal](link_80) hotel. In front of it stood the majestic Cowasji Jehangir Public Hall, which is now the NGMA. The insides of the theatre were as dreamy as the set of Hollywood films screened here,” he says of the Art Deco architecture style that Regal shares with other South Mumbai cinemas like Liberty and Eros. Inaugurated on October 14, 1933 by Mumbai governor Sir Frederick Sykus, Regal was built by film exhibitor Framji Sidhwa and his friend KA Kooka. And it had quite a few firsts to its credit. Asia’s first centrally air-conditioned theatre, it was also the first to introduce Cinemascope and offer basement car parking to its patrons. The reinforced concrete structure built at a lavish cost was conceived by Charles Stevens, son of famous 19th century English architect Fredrick Williams Stevens, while the interiors were designed by Czechoslovakian artist Karl Schara. Old-timers remember the sun ray Cubist motif in orange and jade green in the atrium.   
 For Deepak Rao, retired IPS officer and member of the Bombay Local History Society, Regal stands for an afternoon Arlem beer. While working at the Mumbai police headquarters across the road from the cinema, he’d hop over to its refreshment room that could house no more than six guests.

 Regal’s historic value preceeds its construction, says Rao. “The lane behind Regal is not named Battery Street for nothing. The site at Apollo Bunder on which the cinema stands was owned by the British army, and was occupied by an old saluting battery. When viceroys and VIPs arrived, they were greeted with a gun salute. The British government decided to lease the property in 1926, which is when it was acquired by Mr Sidhwa and Mr Kooka of Globe Theatre Ltd.,” says the 62 year-old.   
 Sidhwa’s life, say documents, was as dramatic as the movies he screened. Born in 1883 in Tarapore, Gujarat, in a middle-class home, he moved to an orphanage in Parel before gaining admission to Bharda New High School, which stands right beside the theatre he would build in 1928 — Capitol at VT. The student of St Xavier’s College had to drop out due to thinning finances and move to Rangoon in 1903 to find a job. Starting out as a clerk in Singer, he later took up an insurance job.   
 It was in 1913 that he established a small syndicate and launched his film exhibition business in Rangoon. Two years later, Globe Theatre Ltd. was born.   
 “Behram Contractor, in one of his essays, said going to the cinema was an art,” says Rao. And Regal played its part.   
 Baghdadi calls it an “experience” — South Bombay movie lovers would book tickets way in advance, dress up in finery and land up at the movies. “There was a soda fountain, a pantry for balcony audiences, and we’d dig into ice cream while musicians would perform live,” he shares.   
 Social worker, champion bridge player and MP Milind Deora’s mother Hema Deora’s memories of Regal stand testimony to Baghdadi’s description. As a 10 year-old in the early 1960s, Deora didn’t understand cinema, but that hardly mattered. “For me, the draw was the ice cream served in the cinema’s restaurant. The cup resembled a wine glass. It was a family affair. I’d wear my best dress, and we’d return home in a tonga,” Deora reminisces.
